articles.title: Remember the frontier AI pause? Chip companies don’t either
articles.body:
This summer, OpenAI paused its largest planned frontier training run after its AI agents accidentally hacked Hugging Face and early evidence suggested that its next model could independently find and exploit security flaws. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing advances in the most powerful AI models, warning that they could be used to launch cyberattacks or become harder for their own creators to control.
Remember the frontier AI pause? Chip companies don’t either
Nvidia and AMD earnings show booming demand. This is why a frontier slowdown might not derail it.
It was a strange moment for the AI boom. The people building the most powerful models were warning about what those models might be capable of, and investors were suddenly wondering what would happen to chip demand if the labs eased up on new models. US chip stocks bore the brunt of the sell-off.
“Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend.”
Despite the hubbub it created, whatever slowdown there was appears to have been short-lived. OpenAI had announced only a two-week pause; it restarted the run 10 days later, at the end of August, though it continued to “temporarily hold back some smaller experimental training runs.” Anthropic released upgraded versions of its Fable and Mythos frontier models in November, touting improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision.
And the companies selling the chips powering those advances are doing better than ever.
Nvidia on Tuesday posted a blockbuster quarter, with data center revenue rising 110 percent from a year ago to $107.6 billion in the three months ended October 25. The chip designer began shipping its most advanced AI computing system, the Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it the “fastest product ramp in the company’s history.” The Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments alone. The racks are already running at CoreWeave, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle. Meta plans to expand Vera Rubin deployments to train and run AI models and agents.
Nvidia name-dropped Anthropic and OpenAI, too. Anthropic has expanded access to Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers and continues to work with Nvidia on future chip designs tailored to its workloads. OpenAI is among the companies adopting Nvidia’s new Vera CPUs.
“Proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic continue to advance the frontier,” Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on the earnings call. She said the company expects major frontier labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its data center revenue this fiscal year. Nvidia also raised its revenue growth forecast for next fiscal year from 70 percent to 75 percent.
Chipmaker AMD, meanwhile, reported its biggest quarter ever earlier this month, with revenue up 45 percent to $13.4 billion. Data center sales drove that growth, nearly doubling to $8.5 billion. OpenAI and Anthropic were among the first customers running workloads on AMD’s new high-end Helios systems, which use its latest MI450 GPUs.
Broadcom, which helps many of the biggest AI companies design their own custom chips, has yet to report earnings. But so far, there’s little sign of a frontier slowdown hurting chip sales.
Of course, even if AI labs were to significantly scale back their training ambitions, it would take a while to show up in chipmakers’ earnings. Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, told The Verge in September that it would take about six months to see the financial effects of a slowdown, owing to existing computing and memory procurement agreements. The impact could show up sooner in orders placed with chip manufacturers like TSMC.
So far, there’s little evidence of that, either: TSMC’s latest sales figures also show continued strength.
But there’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have.
“While one might argue the need for top-end GPUs will reduce with this shift toward inferencing, these workloads will collectively require more compute infrastructure than training,” Shah said. “Overall, it means a net increase in demand for all types of accelerators.”
There’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have.
According to our analysis of the latest data from corporate spending platform Ramp, frontier model families accounted for about 60 percent of token usage among businesses using Ramp in early November — a record high and about three times their share at the start of the year. That includes OpenAI’s Astra and Sol models and Anthropic’s Opus and Fable models.
But even as businesses use more AI, their spending is only growing modestly.
“It’s not really a demand issue though,” Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp, tells The Verge. “By all measures, companies are using more AI.”
Rather, competition among AI model providers is driving down token prices so rapidly that it’s calling OpenAI and Anthropic’s revenue projections into question, Kharazian says.
That could prove beneficial for the companies supplying computing power. On Nvidia’s earnings call, Kress said token prices had fallen nearly 60 percent since May, spurring more usage. Meanwhile, rental prices for Nvidia GPUs across generations have gone up.
Nvidia and AMD are positioning their most powerful chips for both training and inference, including the demanding workloads created by AI agents.
That doesn’t necessarily mean Nvidia will maintain its dominance. As AI companies get more serious about the economics of serving their models to millions of people, they’re increasingly turning to custom chips that can do so more cheaply than general-purpose GPUs. Counterpoint expects shipments of custom AI server processors to surpass those of data center GPUs by 2028.
“Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend,” Shah said.
Indeed, on Nvidia’s earnings call, UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked Kress whether the company would be willing to sacrifice some of its hefty profit margins as frontier labs increasingly invest in custom chips and prioritize computing efficiency. Kress maintained that Nvidia’s systems justify their pricing and reiterated the company’s gross margin outlook.
For companies like Nvidia, the bigger threat may not be that AI companies slow down, but that they find cheaper chips on which to keep going.

articles.title: Bank CEOs, NSA Tell Congress That AI-Driven Patches Are Behind Outages
articles.body:
Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency have told members of Congress that this week’s widespread tech outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by artificial intelligence, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations.
Over the last few days, the country has faced a series of startling tech failures, leading to a pause in all flights nationwide, customers being unable to access their bank accounts and a highly classified communications network at the National Security Agency going down.
While it does not appear that these disruptions were caused by a cyberattack, government and banking officials have told lawmakers that they stem from attempts to fix gaps in cyber defenses identified by AI models, the sources said. The fixes, however, temporarily overwhelmed the systems.
“These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away,” said one congressional official briefed on the matter. “They’re trying to push through a lot of patches all at once — more than the system was designed for.”
Trending
On Monday, banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues. On Tuesday, the NSA said that “scheduled routine maintenance” was responsible for the “temporary degradation” of some of its networks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC on Tuesday that “they’re pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system. ... We’re going to see more of this as new technology rolls out.”
Powerful companies and government agencies have increasingly trained the most powerful AI models on themselves, seeking to identify the vulnerabilities that others may weaponize against them. Once these gaps are identified, they are under immense pressure to patch them as soon as possible, knowing that malicious actors have access to comparable AI tools — or will soon.
This urgency is what has driven a wide range of public- and private-sector actors to rush fixes to their systems faster than they normally would, the sources said. But even entities with large resources, such as the nation’s top banks and the intelligence community, are finding it difficult to do so without accidentally causing outages. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.
The outages rippled across the country this week. The Federal Aviation Administration canceled more than 20,000 flights as a result of the nationwide ground stop, according to The Wall Street Journal. Microsoft experienced a major outage of Outlook.
Microsoft blamed a technical defect for the disruption. It is also unclear what caused the FAA systems to go down.
“There’s some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there’s not an attack. But it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems,” said Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode. “Updating those is going to be a rocky process, and as we get more advanced models this won’t be a one and done thing — we’ll continue to find more vulnerabilities.”
The NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Felicis leads $7.5M bet on Unsiloed AI to make enterprise documents usable by AI agents
articles.body:
As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology.
Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated.
Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work.
Unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also shows where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value.
“The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” said Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.”
Mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology.
Unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he said, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents.
The San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors.
Mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most important parts of a document.
“In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra said. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.”
The technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts.
Supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified.
Unsiloed also claims to have outperformed competing AI document-processing tools on olmOCR-Bench, a public benchmark developed by Allen AI. In tests conducted by the startup, Unsiloed scored 88.0, compared with 66.0 for Reducto’s agentic system and 39.9 for Unstructured. The benchmark covered 1,403 PDF pages and tested how well the systems handled tables, mathematical expressions, scanned documents, and complex layouts.
Unsiloed’s pricing, Mishra said, starts at one cent per page. He asserted that the startup’s approach also helps keep its costs down by directing computing power toward the parts of a document that need the most attention, instead of processing every section in the same way.
Currently, Unsiloed has a headcount of seven people. The startup, Mishra said, plans to use the fresh funding to hire more researchers and engineers, expand its sales efforts and develop proprietary datasets to improve its technology.

articles.title: Nvidia Chair Harvey Jones says board doesn't intend to reinstate Huang as CEO
articles.body:
Nvidia beat on profit and revenue after the bell on Tuesday and issued strong guidance, in the chipmaker's first earnings report since co-founder Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation last week as CEO. The stock rose more than 3% in extended trading.
Here's how the company did compared to analysts' estimates, according to LSEG:
EPS: $2.68 adjusted vs. $2.48 expected
Revenue: $115.84 billion vs. $109.10 billion expected
Revenue more than doubled from $57 billion a year earlier, Nvidia said, a sign of continued strength in its core data center business. The company said revenue this quarter will expand by roughly 90% to about $130 billion, topping the $125.1 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG.
Finance chief Colette Kress is used to addressing Wall Street, but never like this. She's now functioning as interim CEO, meaning her responsibilities go well beyond the key numbers. At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board doesn't intend to bring Huang back as CEO.
The biggest cloud for Nvidia is around its China business after Huang's reported affair with a businesswoman who's allegedly a Chinese spy. The Commerce Department on Monday announced a change that would prevent Nvidia's chips from being rented to Chinese companies entirely, putting revenue at risk.
Nvidia kept with its recent language on China, telling investors in its commentary, "We are not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook."
One of the central questions from investors heading into the call was whether Nvidia would scrap a previous forecast for 70% growth in the fiscal year ending in January 2028. However, Kress raised guidance, saying that Nvidia now expects 75% growth.
Kress said during the Q&A portion of the call that it's "business as usual at Nvidia."
"Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week to support both what we are doing here at earnings, but also supporting all of our different employees around the world," she said. "Remember, we have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap. And I think that's important from a business perspective."
Nvidia's stock is down 24% this month and on Friday wrapped up its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012. The stock has dropped the first two days of this week and is trading at its lowest since July 2025. In addition to the Huang saga, the company is dealing with broader concerns about an AI slowdown and a political shift in Washington, D.C., following this month's midterm elections.
Nvidia's Kress tells Cramer that demand is only increasing
Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress speaks with Jim Cramer during 'Mad Money' on CNBC, Nov. 17, 2026.
CNBC
In her first interview since Huang's abrupt departure, Kress told CNBC's Jim Cramer on Tuesday that, "The most important thing we have seen is growth in the demand that's out there."
Nvidia said it expected 75% growth in the next year, higher than the company's previous forecast of 70%.
"What we need in terms of chips, what we need in terms of advanced packaging or memory, all of that is also coming together," Kress said. "We felt very confident, therefore, that we could establish that we will grow 75% over year over year in terms of fiscal year 28."
Kress was brought in as interim CEO last week after 13 years as Nvidia's CFO. She previously served in financial roles at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments.
The board is in the process of selecting a long-term CEO, hiring executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to lead the hunt, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said on the earnings call.
Jones said the board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Huang said in a statement Tuesday that he's open to returning, and an online petition calling for his reinstatement has nearly 200,000 signatures.
— Kif Leswing and Katie Tarasov
17 Hours Ago
Kress says customers haven't gone anywhere
Kress told Cramer that hyperscalers and other customers aren't going anywhere.
"This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers: that is just not true," she said, adding that "customers continue to be with us."
— Ari Levy
16 Hours Ago
Neocloud stocks up in after hours trading
Neocloud stocks rose in extended trading after Nvidia's earnings call offered confidence in the AI infrastructure buildout. The company beat estimates and lifted its forecast.
The really came despite reports that Nvidia is looking to reel in its backstop agreements that have bolstered the industry. During the earnings call interim CEO Colette Kress said Nvidia would be "rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees" and that the company will remain "disciplined in how we commit capital."
Nvidia stock was up nearly 4% in after-hours trading. However, the stock is way down over the past month, and plunged last week after news broke of ex-CEO Jensen Huang's entanglements with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
— Isabel O'Brien
17 Hours Ago
Gene Munster: Investors should 'look at the bigger picture'
watch now
VIDEO5:3005:30
SEC investigation an 'expected outcome' for Nvidia, says Deepwater's Gene Munster
Gene Munster, managing partner of Deepwater Asset Management, said investors should focus on Nvidia's business outlook as the board searches for a permanent CEO.
"The current business and the outlook is rock solid, and that gives you time...to figure out who the next person is," Munster told CNBC's "Fast Money."
"Investors should take a step back and look at the bigger picture."
Munster also said that while Nvidia's Asia market won't be completely wiped out amid changing security dynamics, geopolitical headwinds will have an impact on Nvidia's growth in the coming year. The Commerce Department moved to close a loophole Monday that allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia computing power located in other countries.
— Caleigh Keating
17 Hours Ago
Kress coming up with Jim Cramer in first interview since Huang exit
Kress is set to appear on CNBC's "Mad Money" with Jim Cramer around 6:30 p.m. ET, in what will be her first interview since Huang's exit.
18 Hours Ago
Jeff Bezos says Nvidia's board should pick an insider, if it doesn't bring Huang back
Jeff Bezos, founder of Amazon and Blue Origin and co-founder and co-CEO of Prometheus and Vik Bajaj, co-founder and co-CEO of Prometheus (not pictured) speak with Semafor's business and finance Editor Liz Hoffman at the Semafor "Silicon Valley & The World" Conference in San Francisco, California, US Nov. 17, 2026.
Manuel Orbegozo | Reuters
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said Nvidia's board should choose an insider to succeed Huang as the chipmaker's CEO, adding that if it were up to him, he "would not hire an outsider."
"Hire from internally," Bezos said at Semafor's "Silicon Valley and The World" conference on Tuesday. "If you don't bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider."
He went on to say, "I think outside CEOs in complex companies have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding, and so I would always think that's a last resort."
Amazon went through its own CEO transition in 2021 when Bezos, who founded the e-commerce and cloud computing juggernaut in 1994, turned over the helm to Andy Jassy.
Bezos remains Amazon's executive chairman, but he now dedicates more of his time to his rocket company Blue Origin and Prometheus, an artificial intelligence startup he co-founded and where he serves as co-CEO.
Bezos contrasted the situation at Nvidia with Amazon's executive changeover, saying, "There has never been a more planful transition."
Asked whether he thinks Huang should return, Bezos said, "I don't know enough of the details."
"What I can tell you for sure is that Jensen is a remarkable guy who founded and built a remarkable company with a lot of hard work and foresight and he deserves a lot of admiration and respect, no matter what," Bezos said.
— Annie Palmer
18 Hours Ago
Susquehanna's Chris Rolland floats idea of Huang coming back as advisor
watch now
VIDEO4:4104:41
Nvidia out with 'very solid report,' says Susquehanna's Chris Rolland
Susquehanna analyst Chris Rolland said he doesn't expect Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang as CEO but wonders whether it might bring him back as a strategic adviser or consultant.
"I think that helps bridge the gap here, and he can give technical and strategic advisory services that I think would be incredibly important to the company," Rolland told CNBC's "Fast Money."
The Nvidia board has not publicly addressed the idea that it would consider bringing Huang on in an advisory or consulting role.
Kress said that it is "business as usual" at Nvidia, and that representatives from TSMC had visited Nvidia this week.
"It's business as usual. We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They're all 100% behind us," Kress said.
— Kif Leswing
18 Hours Ago
Nvidia VP Ian Buck joins the call for questions
To answer analyst questions, Nvidia veteran Ian Buck joined the call.
Buck is a well-respected Nvidia veteran who works on GPU systems and who is viewed by some analysts as a candidate for CEO. He helped create CUDA, the software that allows the company's chips to be used for AI.
— Kif Leswing
18 Hours Ago
Frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic will make up 15% of data center sales this year
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI (L), and Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic
Reuters | Getty Images
Nvidia said it expects major frontier labs to account for about 15% of data center sales this year, a sign that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are increasingly standing up their own infrastructure.
"As frontier models become more capable, adoption and revenue are scaling rapidly, with Anthropic annualized revenue reaching $81 billion at the end of October," Kress said.
— Kif Leswing
18 Hours Ago
Nvidia indicates Hugging Face acquisition still on track
Andrey Rudakov | Bloomberg | Getty Images
In opening remarks, Kress indicated that Nvidia still will acquire Hugging Face, the open-source repository that it agreed to purchase for just under $13 billion in September.
"Together, we will scale its platform and make intelligence more open, more capable and more accessible," Kress said.
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Nvidia said 4 customers represented 47% of sales
Nvidia sells to direct customers — manufacturers, distributors, cloud service providers and frontier labs — and to indirect customers, who buy Nvidia gear from the direct customers.
The company said two direct customers accounted for 18% and 17% of its accounts receivable balance as of the end of October.
Nvidia added in supplemental financial information that in the last three quarters, four direct customers accounted for between 11% and 13% each of total revenue.
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Kress raises fiscal 2028 outlook
Nvidia's Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress poses for a photo in an unknown location.
Nvidia | Via Reuters
In raising the company's outlook for annual growth, Kress said guidance "considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers access to capital."
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Nvidia has not made any payments related to guarantees for OpenAI's Ohio data center
Nvidia said Tuesday that it has $118 billion in guarantees as of Oct. 25, for land, power, shell, and hardware financing, in particular, with an OpenAI project in Ohio.
Nvidia said that its exposure would max out at $105 billion, and then would decline over each 20-year lease term.
"To date, we have not made any payments related to our guarantees," Nvidia said in its CFO commentary.
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Harvey Jones, Nvidia's new board chair, is joining the call
New board chair Harvey Jones joined Kress on Nvidia's earnings call Tuesday, delivering the opening remarks.
He said that Huang had resigned after disclosing personal behavior "inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."
"The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said.
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Nvidia has $32 billion in neocloud committments through 2032
Nvidia said it's helping neoclouds and frontier labs secure the land, power and data center capacity they need to grow, and that the company may share revenue from neoclouds along with the upfront sales of its products, if certain conditions are met.
"Our commitments take effect only if the neoclouds secure financing to purchase the data center infrastructure products and the related compute capacity is deployed, made operational, and accepted by us," Nvidia said in its CFO commentary.
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Nvidia spends billions on memory and data center leases
Nvidia's commitments to secure supply of parts for its chips and systems increased to $390 million from $279 billion in the prior period.
The sharp increase is primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply, the company said in its earnings commentary.
Nvidia data center lease commitments and cloud service agreements came to $102 billion, up from $74 billion in the last quarter.
"Our upcoming data center leases have terms up to twenty years and have not commenced. These leases are expected to commence between the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2033," Kress said in the commentary. "We may assign some of these leases to third parties in the future."
"Our commitments take effect only if the neoclouds secure financing to purchase the data center infrastructure products and the related compute capacity is deployed, made operational, and accepted by us, the company said."
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Nvidia's robots and PCs in-line with Wall Street expectations
CLOiD, the Nvidia-powered humanoid robot by LG, left, on display at the Nvidia Corp. AI Day event in Seoul, South Korea, on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026.
Jean Chung | Bloomberg | Getty Images
Nvidia reported $8.2 billion in third-quarter edge computing revenue, a category that includes robotics- related products as well as its graphics cards for gamers and running AI at home. That topped a StreetAccount estimate of $7.47 billion, and represents 42% annual growth — lower than the company's data center business, but still robust.
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Nvidia spent $28.1 billion on share repurchases during the quarter
Gene Medi | Nurphoto | Getty Images
Nvidia isn't backing down from the $150 billion share repurchase plan it announced in September.
The company said it spent $28.1 billion on buybacks during the quarter.
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Gross margin stays high
Investors have been closely watching Nvidia's gross margin, which has narrowed in recent quarters as the company has piled up supply commitments to build its chips.
But Nvidia beat Wall Street expectations for the critical metric on Tuesday, with non-GAAP gross margin coming in at 74.9%, beating a Street Account estimate of 74%.
Nvidia said that the sequentially declining gross margin was due to the ramping up of production of its Rubin GPUs.
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Kress says that roadmap is on track
Kress said in a statement that the company's roadmap is on track.
"Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress is quoted as saying. "Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater."
— Kif Leswing
19 Hours Ago
Nvidia's data center business beats expectations, doubles in a year
Nvidia's most important business is its data center revenue, which includes the GPU systems it ships to hyperscalers and other data center providers.
Nvidia said it had data center revenue of $107.6 billion, higher than the Street Account estimate of $101.87 billion.
Data center revenue more than doubled from a year ago.
— Kif Leswing
20 Hours Ago
Neoclouds provided some relief last week
watch now
VIDEO3:3803:38
Strong AI demand makes data center, neoclouds attractive: Portfolio Manager
One of the big concerns in the AI trade has been the health of the neoclouds, which rely on the capital markets to fund their expansion and are now facing higher interest rates for future debt.
At least for now, there are no signs of a slowdown. In CoreWeave's earnings report last week, the company said revenue jumped 168% from a year earlier and forecast $13 billion to $13.3 billion in full-year sales, which would be up more than 150% from 2025.
Nebius followed last week by reporting 571% revenue growth.
— Ari Levy
20 Hours Ago
Board lacks recent chip industry experience
FILE: Jensen Huang, co-founder and CEO of Nvidia Corp., speaks during a news conference in Taipei on May 21, 2025. Cheng / AFP) (Photo by I-HWA CHENG/AFP via Getty Images)
I-hwa Cheng | Afp | Getty Images
Huang's departure leaves a void of semiconductor engineering experience on Nvidia's 10-person board of directors, which is made up primarily of financial and business executives.
"I think it's important to have someone on the board who is steeped in experience in high tech," chip analyst Patrick Moorhead wrote in a message to CNBC. "The challenge with bringing somebody in with semiconductor experience is that it brings up a lot of conflicts of interest."
Moorhead said the company could turn to someone who's retired.
Harvey Jones, who has served on Nvidia's board since the company's founding in 1993 and is now board chair, has technical experience that predates his current position managing Square Wave Ventures. Jones served as CEO of chip design company Synopsys and co-founded Daisy Systems and Tensilica.
When Jones stepped down as Synopsys CEO in 1994, Nvidia hadn't announced its first chip yet.
Mark Stevens, another longtime board member, held technical roles at Intel and Hughes Aircraft before moving into venture capital.
Nvidia board members collectively have a median of 24 years since their last operating roles, according to industry podcast host Phil McKinney. That's the highest among companies that he tracks, followed by AMD, whose board members have a median of 11 years since holding an operating role.
— Katie Tarasov
21 Hours Ago
Wall Street not worried about this fiscal year — or next
watch now
VIDEO6:2906:29
Morning Call Sheet: Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO and Fed rate outlook
With Nvidia three-fourths of the way through fiscal 2027, most analysts say that, from a financial perspective, the real impact of Huang's departure won't be felt until the end of fiscal 2028. That's because contracted revenue through next fiscal year is largely in the books.
Nvidia is expected to show revenue growth of 90% in fiscal 2027, followed by expansion the following year of 70%, when sales will top $690 billion, according to LSEG's consensus analyst estimate. Analysts expect earnings per share to climb to $15.73 from $9.28 this year.
Beyond that, there's plenty of uncertainty.
— Ari Levy
22 Hours Ago
Gerstner says he has confidence in Kress
Brad Gerstner, founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, speaking at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World conference in San Francisco on Nov. 16th, 2026.
CNBC
After publishing a letter on Friday urging the board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia" that could include bringing Huang back, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that he has confidence in Kress.
"Jensen was an extreme visionary in the industry, nobody questions that," Gerstner told CNBC's Scott Wapner. "I think the company is very capable of making the trains run on time day to day."
— Ari Levy
21 Hours Ago
Hyperscaler customers mostly held capex forecasts in check
Jaque Silva | Nurphoto | Getty Images
Nvidia's big hyperscaler customers — Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft — all reported quarterly results last month, and mostly kept their guidance for capital expenditures in check.
Alphabet maintained its full-year capex forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion, while Amazon stuck with $220 billion. Meta narrowed the range for its full-year guidance to $135 billion to $145 billion, lifting the bottom of the range by $5 billion. Microsoft reduced its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion
— Ari Levy
22 Hours Ago
Nvidia employees go public with their feelings after Huang exit
Nvidia employees are posting publicly about Huang's exit, with at least one senior research engineer writing that it led to his own decision to leave.
"Jensen's vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay, Shiqin "Darrell" Dai, a robotics engineer in Shanghai, wrote on social media over the weekend. "His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close."
Dai told CNBC in a message Monday that he is "still in a process of leaving."
Jane Polak Scowcraft posted on LinkedIn on Sunday, "This has been the most challenging week of my career. Jensen was more than just a CEO."
Scowcraft, a senior director of generative AI data strategy, said she is "proud, and still a little in awe, that I get to work here." She called Huang "a champion of AI, open source and open data, and everyone that worked at NVIDIA."
— Katie Tarasov
22 Hours Ago
OpenAI announces GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, two new AI models
OpenAI, one of Nvidia's largest customers, announced two new AI models on Tuesday: GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol.
GPT-6.2 Astra is OpenAI's most advanced model for "complex professional work," while GPT-6.2 Sol is its most "versatile model for everyday work," the company said.
"Both models deliver better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done within your usage limits," OpenAI said in a blog post.
The model releases come as the safety and security practices at OpenAI are facing intense scrutiny. California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued the company on Monday for allegedly endangering the public by developing advanced AI models without adequate safeguards and monitoring.
In July, OpenAI disclosed that its models escaped containment and breached the company Hugging Face, which rattled industry researchers and prompted OpenAI to pledge to invest more in safety. The company pulled the release of GPT-6.1 Astra in September after determining that it did not meet adequate safety standards.
OpenAI said Tuesday that it's deploying GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol with its "strongest safeguards to date." The company said it has strengthened the system it uses to monitor models, and built more controls into its model development and training.
—Ashley Capoot
23 Hours Ago
Amazon CEO Jassy: 'I don't foresee a day where we're not partners with Nvidia'
watch now
VIDEO3:2103:21
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy: 'I don’t foresee a day where we are not partners with Nvidia'
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said Tuesday he expects to keep doing business with Nvidia, as the chipmaker grapples with the fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation.
"I don't foresee a day where we're not partners with Nvidia," Jassy said in an interview with CNBC's Scott Wapner. "I think they have amazing products. I think we're gonna always have customers who want to run Nvidia in our infrastructure."
Jassy, who spoke on the sidelines of Semafor's "Silicon Valley and The World" conference, said he has "deep respect" for Jensen Huang and Nvidia.
"I know they're, you know, I don't know all the details of what's happened, but I know they're talking through it, and we'll see what happens," Jassy said.
Amazon is one of Nvidia's largest customers, deploying the company's high-end chips across its sprawling data center footprint. The companies deepened their partnership in August, with Amazon committing to buy 2 million Nvidia graphics processing units, just a few months after it ordered 1 million Nvidia chips.
At the same time, Amazon has been investing heavily in building its own silicon, including its Trainium AI chips, which are designed to be a direct competitor to Nvidia's popular Blackwell.
Last month, Jassy spoke bullishly of Amazon's in-house chips business, and said the company plans to make its Trainium chips externally available for the first time beginning in "late 2027."
"We're gonna have customers who want our silicon, we're going to have customers that want Nvidia silicon, and there may be others too," Jassy said.
— Annie Palmer
23 Hours Ago
Stock has gotten very cheap relative to its peers
With the recent stock slump, Nvidia's price-to-earnings ratio for the next 12 months has dropped to 10.84, according to FactSet. That's by far the lowest among the tech megacaps and is roughly one-third AMD's forward P/E ratio of 30.4.
— Ari Levy
24 Hours Ago
China condemns U.S. closure of chip export control loopholes, threatens countermeasures
watch now
VIDEO3:5603:56
Trump arrives in the Philippines for ASEAN summit amid China trade tensions
China's Ministry of Commerce said Tuesday it "firmly opposes" the U.S. government's move to tighten export controls on advanced chips.
The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule that would require data center operators in countries including Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand to obtain a U.S. government license before exporting advanced AI chips.
The rule seeks to crack down on companies that have circumvented U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure from third countries.
U.S. agencies confirmed Monday that they initiated an investigation into Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that is suspected of helping to ship advanced AI chips to China, violating U.S. export controls. Megaspeed was once led by Alice Huang, who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and who is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence.
The draft regulation "disrupts the stability of global semiconductor industrial and supply chains," a commerce ministry spokesperson said in a statement, translated by CNBC.
"China is strongly dissatisfied with and firmly opposes this," the spokesperson said.
China threatened to take countermeasures if the U.S. doesn't "return to the correct track" of "consultation and cooperation."
"If the US side insists on going its own way, China will take countermeasures and firmly safeguard its national sovereignty, security, and development interests," the spokesperson said.
— Annie Palmer
Tue, Nov 17 202611:41 AM EST
Huang says he’s open to returning to Nvidia in first statement since resignation
Huang issued his first statement on Tuesday since resigning as CEO, and he signaled a willingness to return to Nvidia.
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said.
Sources told CNBC Monday that the board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. The board is focused on the national security investigation, a person familiar with the matter said.
Huang said he made "serious mistakes" in his personal life and "created problems" for Nvidia's board that he deeply regrets, according to the statement. He added that he is "committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
—Ashley Capoot
Tue, Nov 17 202611:08 AM EST
Two days until Anthropic debut
CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei arrives for a luncheon for tech leaders in the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., US, September 29, 2026.
Kevin Lamarque | Reuters
While Tuesday's earnings report is a big event for Nvidia and the AI industry, attention will quickly be turning to Thursday, when Anthropic is looking to hit the Nasdaq in a landmark IPO.
Anthropic is likely to price above the current range of $70 to $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
Nvidia, like a number of its tech peers, has a sizable stake in Anthropic, and is pouring in more money at the IPO price.
Anthropic is also a heavy user of Nvidia's chips through deals it has with SpaceX, Nscale, Lambda and other cloud providers.
In its prospectus, Anthropic calls out Nvidia, AMD, Google and Amazon as its chip providers.
— Ari Levy
Tue, Nov 17 202610:33 AM EST
Is demand still accelerating?
watch now
VIDEO4:0204:02
Fundamentals will prevail after Nvidia story settles, says Defiance ETFs' Jablonski
As the company powering the AI boom, Nvidia's earnings have been viewed by some in the industry as a proxy for overall AI demand.
Huang said in August that "demand was accelerating." Kress echoed the point, saying, "Incredibly, we are seeing demand acceleration even at our scale."
But some investors are worried about how long Nvidia's commitments to shareholders, customers and partners will last, and are eager for an update on demand signals.
Morgan Stanley analysts cut their estimates for calendar 2027 and 2028 data center sales by about 10% on the Huang news saying, "faced with some uncertainty and multiple downgrades, we would rather err on the side of being too conservative."
Nvidia also has made significant commitments to secure the supply it needs to build chips.
In its most recent filing, Nvidia said it committed to $92 billion in supply and capacity for the rest of this fiscal year, $87 billion in the fiscal year ending January 2028, and $88 billion the following year.
— Kif Leswing
Tue, Nov 17 202610:17 AM EST
Nvidia's board forms committee to oversee national security, export controls
Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images
Nvidia announced Tuesday that its board has established a committee overseeing national security and export controls, as the company faces growing scrutiny around its business dealings in southeast Asia and China.
The committee will be responsible for board-level oversight of Nvidia's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management, the company said.
Former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has highlighted Nvidia's relationships with Asian partners and heightened concerns that China could circumvent export controls by renting Nvidia's advanced chips through middleman companies.
Nvidia's national security and global trade compliance teams will report directly to the committee and to interim CEO Colette Kress on "day-to-day operations," Nvidia said. The committee will meet "at least quarterly," the company added.
"NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges," Harvey C. Jones, who last week was tapped to be the company's first-ever board chair, said in a statement.
Jones said Nvidia is committed to working with government and industry partners on developing a "robust framework" to "safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation."
— Annie Palmer
Tue, Nov 17 20269:51 AM EST
Nvidia shares attempt a rebound in trading Tuesday
Shares of Nvidiatried to rebound at the opening bell, after days of steep declines amid the fallout from Huang's resignation. Shares traded largely flat Tuesday morning.
Nvidia's stock fell 4% on Monday, closing at its lowest level since July 1, 2025.
Nvidia stock chart
— Caleigh Keating
Tue, Nov 17 20269:51 AM EST
U.S. agencies confirm investigation into Megaspeed
The logo of data center company Megaspeed International is pictured at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on November 10, 2026.
Taryn Ng | Afp | Getty Images
The Justice and Commerce Departments announced late Monday that they are investigating Megaspeed, the Singaporean computing company at the center of the Nvidiaspy scandal.
In a joint release posted on X, the agencies said they began probing Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" after detecting suspicious activity.
The announcement comes as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced growing criticism that he didn't do enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's advanced chips into China, violating U.S. export rules.
Megaspeed was once led by Alice Huang, the woman with whom former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair and who is reportedly believed by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy.
Investigators in May 2025 requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list, the agencies said.
That month, agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, along with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted checks at Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang.
"Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed," the statement said.
— Annie Palmer
Tue, Nov 17 20269:33 AM EST
Will growth still come from neoclouds?
Former President and CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang speaks on AI at the return of American manufacturing at the Hill and Valley Forum at the U.S. Capitol on April 30, 2025 in Washington, DC.
Kevin Dietsch | Getty Images
During the AI boom, Huang has been deeply involved in creating a new class of companies called neoclouds, which competed with Nvidia's hyperscaler customers.
Huang put a lot of importance on supporting the neoclouds, saying over the summer that their business would help drive Nvidia's growth going forward.
But Nvidia is more than just a supplier of chips to that market. It's also a major investor and financier in the space, and Huang has been integral in deciding which companies got chips first. In August, Huang announced a program on CNBC to help the ecosystem raise financing from a group of major financial firms.
It's unclear whether Kress has the same ability to rally Wall Street or to engage in Huang's level of creative dealmaking.
— Kif Leswing
Tue, Nov 17 20268:53 AM EST
What's the real size of the China business?
watch now
VIDEO0:5700:57
Megaspeed launches internal inquiry as Bessent calls for ‘dramatic shakeup’ at Nvidia
Nvidia has insisted in recent quarters that it gets essentially no data center sales from China, but Huang's involvement with a Megaspeed executive has highlighted a nuance that could end up being critical.
Sales to some data centers, especially in Southeast Asia, may have been primarily intended for rentals to Chinese companies. That's what some in Washington allege about Megaspeed.
Culper Research, a short-selling research firm that published a note on Nvidia's "China problem" in May, alleges that 20% of Nvidia's fiscal 2026 compute revenue was "driven by China."
The Department of Commerce moved to close the rental loophole on Monday, putting that kind of revenue at risk.
Nvidia has denied any physical diversion, and said it has no evidence that any such activity has taken place. But that was before last week's scandal.
In a statement on Sunday, a Megaspeed representative said the cloud provider is conducting a thorough internal investigation.
— Kif Leswing
Tue, Nov 17 20268:19 AM EST
Analysts slash price targets
Following Huang's admission of an extramarital affair on Nov. 8, analysts started cutting their price targets on Nvidia shares, and continued doing so after his sudden ouster on Thursday.
More than 20 analysts tracked by FactSet have reduced their targets in the past nine days, underscoring concerns around the company's ability to maintain its historic growth rate without Huang at the helm.
"We believe ex-CEO Jensen was viewed as the global dealmaker 'AI banker', and key innovator," analysts at Mizuho wrote in a report on Sunday. They lowered their price target to $220 from $250, due in part to their view that the change at the top "adds a 6-7-month management overhang."
— Ari Levy
Tue, Nov 17 20268:18 AM EST
Disappointed Huang fans
Jensen Huang, former chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., left, and US President Donald Trump during a meeting with tech executives on artificial intelligence in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026.
Tierney L. Cross | Bloomberg | Getty Images
Many in the tech world, including Elon Musk, have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO. President Trump said he'd be open to it.
But Huang currently has no role with Nvidia, either as CEO or board member, and the board appears unmoved by outside pressure, so far at least. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.

articles.title: Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy
articles.body:
Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy
On Tuesday, November 24, 2026, Quad9 will stop answering DNS queries from France. Quad9 is the Swiss non-profit behind the free 9.9.9.9 resolver, which blocks malware and phishing domains. It is not leaving because of costs or lack of users. It is leaving because a Paris court fined it for refusing to block a list of pirate sports-streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With around 20 similar cases still pending in France, leaving the country is the only option Quad9 can afford.
Cloudflare, which runs the competing 1.1.1.1 resolver, called the departure "a canary in the coal mine", and the post reached the front page of Hacker News. In that thread, Quad9's CTO John Todd asked readers to write "a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path", with plenty of sources, and to send it to policymakers. This is our attempt. Every claim below links to a primary document, a court ruling, or contemporaneous reporting.
What Quad9 is, and why it matters
A DNS resolver turns a name like example.com into an IP address your computer can connect to. Most people use their ISP's resolver without knowing it. A public resolver is one anyone can point their device or network at instead, such as Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Cisco's OpenDNS, or Quad9's 9.9.9.9.
Quad9 has a few properties that make it unusual:
- It is a non-profit. It was founded in 2017 by the Global Cyber Alliance, IBM, and Packet Clearing House, and moved its legal seat to Zürich in 2021, hosted by SWITCH, specifically so that its privacy promises would be backed by Swiss law. As John Todd put it at the time: "Privacy policies which are not backed by law are empty promises."
- Security filtering is its main purpose. Quad9 refuses to resolve domains that threat-intelligence feeds flag as malware, phishing, or botnet infrastructure. Its about page claims 670 million+ blocks a day across 230+ resolver clusters in over 110 countries.
- It keeps no user records. Quad9 does not know who its users are, and that is the point.
Organisations have come to depend on it. Mullvad shut down its own public encrypted DNS service on November 2, 2026 and moved Mullvad Browser users with default settings to Quad9, funding Quad9 instead. (Mullvad Browser users in France will now be migrated to a resolver that disappears three weeks later.) Quad9's announcement lists dozens of French networks it sees traffic from, including the interministerial digital directorate DINUM, France Travail, CEA, Institut Pasteur, RENATER, EDF, SNCF, AP-HM hospitals in Marseille, France Télévisions, Thales, and Airbus's Stormshield. Quad9 can't tell any of them it is leaving. As Cloudflare points out, when a resolver disappears, users don't see an error message. "Their Internet will simply stop working."
How France got here
The law: Article L.333-10 of the Code du sport
The legal basis for all of this is Article L.333-10 of the French sports code. It was created by Law 2021-1382 of October 25, 2021, the same law that merged HADOPI and the CSA into the new regulator Arcom. L.333-10 lets a sports rightsholder go to the president of the Paris judicial court and obtain "dynamic" blocking orders, meaning orders that cover sites already identified plus new mirror domains notified later through Arcom, against "toute personne susceptible de contribuer à y remédier" (any person able to help stop the infringement).
That last phrase is what puts DNS resolvers in scope. In July 2026, Parliament passed Law 2026-725 on professional sport, which amended L.333-10 and added an automated real-time blocking system run by Arcom. TorrentFreak reported that under the new system "ARCOM's agents no longer approve each block in advance." Quad9 called it "recklessly dangerous."
The cases: from ISPs to everyone
The timeline shows how the circle of targets has widened:
The ruling itself
The 21 October judgment is short and worth reading. A few details matter:
- The €580,000 figure was beIN's request, not the penalty. beIN asked for €10,000 per day per domain still reachable; across 58 domains that is €580,000 a day. The judge set €1,000 a day in total, running until the end of the WTA season on November 14.
- The judge used Quad9's malware filtering against it. Quad9 argued it could not implement geolocated blocking. The court (para. 16) replied that Quad9 "appears to contradict itself" because it already "applies automated filtering strictly limited to cybersecurity to neutralise malicious domains on a global scale." The fact that a resolver can drop a name for everyone was treated as proof it can drop a name for France.
- Refusing to try was enough. Paragraph 18: "Bound by an obligation of means, the Quad9 foundation states that it implements none in order to execute the decision. This circumstance alone justifies the imposition of a penalty."
€1,000 a day for three weeks is survivable, about €24,000. Twenty more cases like it, each running for a full football season with ever-growing domain lists and Arcom's new automated system feeding them, is not. Quad9 says: "Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases."
Why Quad9 can't just comply
Quad9 is often asked why it doesn't just block the domains. It has three options, and none of them work.
1. Block globally. This is what Quad9 did for Canal+ in December 2024 and what DNS4EU does today. It means a French court decides what a user in Brazil, Kenya or Germany can resolve, for the commercial benefit of one company. Quad9's announcement asks how France would react if other nations imposed their laws on French users through DNS. The answer is obvious, and the reverse should be too. Nothing limits this to sports either: once global blocking is accepted, every court in every country can add names to everyone's resolver.
2. Geo-block France. Quad9 has already tried this, in Germany. In the Sony Music v. Quad9 case, Quad9 used geoIP blocking for German users while the case continued. Sony's lawyers used a VPN to reach the content "from Germany" anyway, the court agreed this was non-compliance, and Quad9 was fined for contempt. GeoIP is a probabilistic guess about where an IP address is, not a legal fact about where a person is. A resolver that keeps no user records has no reliable way to define a "French user." As Quad9 told TorrentFreak: "There is no legally useful way for us to define a French user." Even the French order is geographically complicated: heise notes it covers the overseas departments and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon but excludes New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and French Polynesia.
3. Pay and fight. Quad9 won in Germany. The Dresden Higher Regional Court held in December 2023 that DNS resolvers get the same liability privilege as access providers, and the German civil rights group GFF said "the judgement puts the onus on rights holders." But winning took "several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time," and the opposition, in Quad9's words, "has more lawyers than we have money and time." As Quad9 wrote in 2025, compliance costs that are routine overhead for Google are, "for small, mission-driven nonprofits like Quad9, … an existential threat."
That leaves leaving.
Why DNS blocking doesn't work
The argument against resolver blocking isn't only about Quad9's survival. Even on its own terms, it does not do what the rightsholders want.
It doesn't remove anything. The DNS only holds pointers. Quad9's Dresden write-up puts it this way: "The DNS does not contain content - it is a system designed for delivery only of pointers." The pirate server stays online and keeps serving everyone who reaches it some other way. The Internet Society's 2025 guide for legal professionals says the same thing.
It takes seconds to bypass. Quad9 notes there are thousands of other open resolvers. Users can also run their own, or use encrypted DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484), which looks like ordinary web traffic. Arcom's own December 2025 study for the National Assembly says 20% of French internet users already use an alternative DNS resolver and 29% use a VPN. Quad9 compares DNS blocking to "holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert."
It is blunt. DNS works at the level of whole domains. A resolver can't block one infringing stream on a shared host without blocking everything else on that name. The IAB's RFC 7754, the IETF's standard reference on blocking and filtering, says: "From a technical perspective, there are no perfect or even good solutions -- there is only least bad." ICANN's security committee revisited the question in SAC127, "DNS Blocking Revisited" (2025), warning implementers to minimise overblocking and avoid affecting users outside their jurisdiction. France's own registry operator, AFNIC, made the core point years ago in its scientific council's report on the consequences of DNS filtering: "Le DNS n'a pas été conçu pour filtrer les contenus." (The DNS was not designed to filter content.)
It is opaque. When a resolver is forced to lie, the user sees a site that doesn't load. They have no way to tell whether the site is down, their network is broken, or a court ordered the block. There is a standard for being honest about this: RFC 8914 Extended DNS Errors defines code 16, "Censored", for answers withheld "due to an external requirement imposed by an entity other than the operator." But nothing in the French orders requires resolvers to use it.
Blocking at scale causes real collateral damage. France is not the only test case. Italy's Piracy Shield system blocked Google Drive for much of the country in October 2024. A RIPE Labs study of Piracy Shield found more than 500 unrelated sites blocked and concluded that "IP-level blocking is an indiscriminate tool with consequences that outweigh its benefits." In Spain, LaLiga's IP blocking of shared Cloudflare addresses knocked innocent sites offline every match day, leading Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince to call the approach "bonkers". The same RIPE study found most European piracy is hosted in Europe, which is where enforcement belongs: at the hosting provider.
Measured by its own goals, the French system has a mixed record. Arcom reports 12,606 sports domains blocked since 2022, 6,496 of them in 2025 alone (up 71%), while piracy fell 4% in 2025 and 34% since 2021. The number of blocks is growing much faster than piracy is shrinking, and Arcom's figures don't separate the effect of resolver blocking from ISP blocking. Every one of those domains has to be found, blocked, and then found again when it reappears under a new name. OONI's 2025 measurement of French ISP blocking found that of 542 domains tested, 291 were blocked by at least one ISP but only 132 by all four. The European Commission's own 2025 assessment of its live-events piracy recommendation concluded the effects "have been limited and have not allowed to significantly curb the volume of online piracy of live events."
What France loses
Driving Quad9 out of France doesn't hurt pirates at all. The people who lose are the ones who chose a resolver for security.
- French users lose a malware filter. Quad9 exists to stop people resolving phishing and malware domains. Users who move to an unfiltered resolver, or to their ISP's resolver, lose that protection. Users who move to an unknown free resolver may be trading it for one that sells their browsing data. As Cloudflare puts it, "Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web."
- Critical infrastructure may break silently. Hospitals, utilities and local authorities on Quad9's list will lose DNS if their IT teams miss the announcement. Embedded devices with 9.9.9.9 hard-coded may be hard to fix.
- The choice of resolvers shrinks. OpenDNS left France in 2024, and Quad9 leaves now. An Internet Society report cited by TorrentFreak warned that small and non-profit resolvers are the most likely to be pushed out, leaving the field to the largest companies, which can afford to fight or to build per-country infrastructure. Cloudflare can satisfy the court by blocking at its CDN; Quad9 has only a resolver.
- France's own digital sovereignty goals suffer. France promotes privacy-respecting European infrastructure, yet its courts are driving out a Swiss privacy-focused non-profit while US giants remain.
It's not just France
Quad9 is the clearest casualty so far, but the same process is underway across Europe.
- Belgium: DAZN obtained an order against Cloudflare, Google and Cisco in March 2025, and OpenDNS left Belgium in April 2025 before returning when the order against Cisco was suspended. In August 2026, the Brussels business court upheld the core of the order, with fines of €100,000 per match day capped at €20 million per company. Cisco says its public DNS "does not allow for the implementation of selective, geolocated and dynamic blocking as required by the order." Cloudflare, Google and Cisco have appealed ahead of the January 2027 deadline.
- Italy: AGCOM fined Cloudflare €14.2 million in January 2026, 1% of its global revenue, for not blocking via 1.1.1.1. Prince threatened to pull servers and free services from Italy: "Play stupid games, win stupid prizes."
- Spain: A Barcelona court upheld LaLiga's right to block Cloudflare IP addresses.
- Germany is the counter-example. Courts there rejected resolver blocking for both Quad9 and Cloudflare.
- The EU level: A study commissioned by the European Parliament's legal affairs committee proposes a binding regulation that would require blocking within 30 minutes across DNS resolvers, VPNs and CDNs. John Todd's warning on Hacker News is that "the EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region."
That is why France matters beyond France. If its model becomes the EU template, every public resolver in Europe will face the choice Quad9 faced: lie to all users worldwide, build unreliable geolocation infrastructure, or leave.
The counter-arguments
The Hacker News discussion wasn't one-sided, and the counter-arguments deserve answers.
"Hosting providers are unreachable, so courts move up the chain." One commenter argued that pirate hosts are bulletproof and ignore courts, so going after the intermediaries is the only lever left. Another asked the Quad9 CTO directly where the problem should be attacked. This is the strongest point. But the RIPE data shows most of the hosting is in Europe and within reach of European courts, and the commenter's logic leads to blocking at the last link in the chain that cannot fight back. That is not the same as the link that can actually stop the infringement.
"Friction works. Most people won't bother to switch." Some argued that DNS blocking is good because it nudges the majority while staying easy to bypass for those who know how. The Paris Court of Appeal used essentially this reasoning. But Arcom's numbers say a fifth of French users already use alternative DNS, the friction is gone the moment one person changes a router setting for a household, and the cost is paid by resolvers that never had anything to do with piracy.
"Cloudflare is a hypocrite." Several commenters pointed out that Cloudflare's CDN fronts many pirate sites. That may be true, and it is an argument about Cloudflare's CDN, which French courts can already reach and have. It says nothing about whether a resolver should lie.
"The yellow pages would be held responsible." One commenter asked whether we'd accept a phone directory that kept listing a drug dealer's new address. The analogy fails because a resolver is not a curated directory. It's closer to the operator who connects you to whatever number you dial. Quad9 has "no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites." Making the operator liable for every number dialled is how you end up with no operator.
What you can do
If you use Quad9 in France, check whether you do at on.quad9.net, and switch resolvers before November 24. Check routers, VPN configs, DHCP settings, Pi-hole upstreams, and any devices with 9.9.9.9 or 149.112.112.112 hard-coded. Whatever you switch to, read its privacy policy first.
If you're in France or the EU, do what John Todd asked: write something long-form, ideally in French, make it indexable, and send it to your representatives. Quad9 specifically suggests telling Arcom that its mandate is to balance rightsholders' interests against citizens' digital rights, and that "balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage."
If you work on infrastructure, push for transparency wherever blocking does happen. RFC 8914's "Censored" error code exists so users can tell a court-ordered block from a broken network.
If you can afford it, Quad9 accepts donations for its legal defence. Its appeal against the May order is still pending at the Paris Court of Appeal.
The canary
Quad9 put it this way: "Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly." The French system started with football. It now covers tennis, rugby, MotoGP and Formula 1, has expanded from ISPs to resolvers, VPNs, CDNs and search engines, and runs through an automated system in which no human approves each block. Each step was reasonable on its own. Together, they have pushed a non-profit security service out of the country while the piracy continues.
The sports-rights industry has a real problem. DNS resolvers are the wrong place to solve it, and France is about to find out what the internet looks like when the trustworthy resolvers leave first.
