articles.title: The x86 CPU: From 4004 to 486
articles.body:
We already covered the main ideas behind Real Mode & Protected Mode in one of our previous posts. This article will build on those concepts and take a deeper look at the history and evolution of the x86 family of CPUs. But rather than simply looking at the innovations introduced with each new chip, we need to understand how the architecture accumulated over time, from its origins in the early 70s up until the launch of the 486.
Every time a new student starts learning x86 assembler with us, it's not rare to hear them complain that many aspects of the instruction set look arbitrary. An accumulator that some instructions insist on, a base register that is the only one allowed to point at memory, a parity flag nobody seems to use, and an addressing scheme that adds two 16-bit numbers together in a very strange way.
The majority of teaching resources out there will help you write your first lines of x86 code, assemble it, link it, and as proceed as soon as the output matches what you were expecting. I try to always explain the evolution of the x86 family of CPUs, so every aspect of our code makes a little bit more sense.
None of these things are arbitrary, of course. Each one is a decision someone made under pressure, usually to keep old software running on a new chip. If you want to really understand x86 (and especially if you want to program a 486 under DOS), the best place to start is not the 486 manual. It's the story.
Here is the family tree we're going to walk through:
A table like this makes the evolution look neat and planned. It wasn't. Between these rows there are cancelled projects, a customer who walked away from its own chip, a stopgap that was supposed to last a couple of years, a sales campaign, a keyboard controller wired into the address bus, and a lawsuit.
Let's travel back to 1969 and see how it all happened!
A Calculator Chip: The 4004
The story starts with a Japanese calculator company. In 1969, Busicom asked Intel (then a young memory company) to build a set of custom chips for a new printing calculator. Instead of designing many single-purpose chips, Intel's team proposed something more general: a small programmable processor that would run the calculator's logic from ROM.
The result was the 4004, released on November 15, 1971, and designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima. It had 2,300 transistors, ran at about 740 kHz, and could address 4 KB of program ROM.
The most important line in the 4004's story is not technical, though. Busicom had paid for the design and owned the rights. When Busicom ran into financial trouble in 1971, Faggin convinced Intel's CEO Bob Noyce to lower the chip's price in exchange for Intel getting out of the exclusivity deal. Intel paid back Busicom's $60,000 development costs and won the right to sell the chip to anyone (outside the calculator market).
That deal is why "a microprocessor" became something Intel could sell, rather than a part buried inside one calculator.
The Terminal That Didn't Want Its CPU: The 8008
At almost the same time, a second customer walked through Intel's door. In late 1969, Computer Terminal Corporation (CTC, later called Datapoint) asked Intel to build a chip for a programmable terminal called the Datapoint 2200.
This detail matters a lot: Intel did not design the instruction set of this chip. CTC's engineers Victor Poor and Harry Pyle did. They had already built the Datapoint 2200's processor out of dozens of discrete TTL chips, and they wanted Intel to squeeze that same design onto one piece of silicon.
Intel was slow. Texas Instruments also tried to build the chip, but its samples were buggy and rejected. Meanwhile, CTC shipped the Datapoint 2200 in 1970 with its TTL processor anyway, and later moved on to a faster design. In the end, CTC voted to walk away from the project and leave the design to Intel instead of paying the $50,000 contract. Intel renamed it the 8008 and released it in April 1972 with 3,500 transistors and 16 KB of addressable memory.
So the ancestor of every x86 chip was designed by a terminal company, for a terminal, and then rejected by that terminal company. And two of the terminal's habits are still inside your PC today.
Why x86 is Little-Endian
The Datapoint 2200 processed numbers one bit at a time (a bit-serial design). If you're adding two numbers one bit at a time, you want to start with the lowest bit, because that's where the carry starts. So it made sense to store the lowest byte first in memory.
The 8008 copied the Datapoint's design, the 8080 kept compatibility with the 8008, and the 8086 kept compatibility with the 8080. Stephen Morse, the architect of the 8086, put it this way in his history of the early Intel processors:
"This inverted storage, which was to haunt all processors evolved from the 8008, was a result of compatibility with the Datapoint bit-serial processor."
That's why, on your 486 (and even in a more modern Core i9), this instruction:
mov DWORD ptr [buffer], 12345678h
...stores the bytes 78 56 34 12 in memory.
Why x86 Has a Parity Flag
The second habit is the parity flag (PF), which tells you if the result of the last operation had an even number of 1 bits. It's one of those flags that beginners look at and wonder who on earth needs it.
The answer is: a terminal does! Morse again: "This permits testing for transmission errors, an obviously useful function for a CRT terminal." Data arriving over a serial line often carried a parity bit, and the Datapoint needed a fast way to check it.
Fifty years later, PF is still bit 2 of the x86 FLAGS register.
The 8080 and the Birth of the PC Hobby
The 8008 was slow and awkward, so Intel designed a much better successor. The 8080 was released in April 1974, with Federico Faggin as its primary architect and Masatoshi Shima on the detailed design. It had about 4,500 transistors, ran at 2 MHz, and could address 64 KB of memory.
The 8080 was not binary compatible with the 8008, but it kept the same register set and the same "flavor." More importantly, it added several things you will recognize as an x86 programmer:
- Register pairs: B and C could be used together as the 16-bit pair BC, and the same for DE and HL
- The HL pair as the main way to point at memory (MOV A, M reads the byte at address HL)
- A real 16-bit stack pointer
- A separate I/O space with 256 ports, accessed with IN and OUT
That separate I/O space is the reason why, many years later, VGA registers live at "port 3C8h" instead of at a memory address.
The 8080 powered the Altair 8800 and became the standard CPU for CP/M, the most popular operating system for small business computers in the late 70s. Suddenly, there was a lot of 8080 software out there.
And then Intel got some serious competition. Faggin and Shima left Intel and went to Zilog, where they built the Z80: a chip that could run 8080 machine code, but was faster, cheaper to build a computer around, and had more instructions. The Z80 started eating Intel's market.
The 8085: A Quiet Hint of What Was Coming
Intel's answer was the 8085, released in March 1976. The "5" in the name refers to its biggest selling point: it needed a single +5 V power supply, while the 8080 needed +5 V, -5 V, and +12 V.
To fit everything into a 40-pin package, the 8085 also multiplexed its bus: the same eight pins carried the low byte of the address first, and then the data. Remember this trick, because the 8086 uses it too.
There's a lovely footnote here: the 8085 had 12 new instructions, but Intel made a last-minute decision to document only 2 of them. The reason? To keep things simple for the next chip, which was already being designed. That chip was the 8086.
The Stopgap That Took Over the World: The 8086
In the mid 70s, Intel's big bet for the future was not the 8086. It was the iAPX 432, a very ambitious processor designed with object-oriented programming and high-level languages in mind. The 432 was late, and with the Z80 taking customers away, Intel needed something to sell in the meantime.
So, in May 1976, Intel started the 8086 project as a temporary product. Stephen Morse was the principal architect, Jim McKevitt and John Bayliss were the lead hardware engineers, and Bill Pohlman managed the project. The 8086 was released on June 8, 1978.
The brief was clear: the new chip had to address more than 64 KB, do 16-bit arithmetic, and (this is the important part) make it easy for existing 8080 software to move over.
Source Compatibility, Not Binary Compatibility
The 8086 cannot run 8080 machine code. Instead, Intel aimed for source compatibility: you could take your 8080 assembly program and translate it, line by line, into 8086 assembly. Intel even shipped a translator called CONV86 (available from 1978) to do this automatically. Morse described the goal like this: "the 8080 register set and instruction set appear as logical subsets of the 8086 registers and instructions."
For that translation to work, every 8080 register needed an obvious home in the 8086. And this is where the 8086's register names come from:
Here's a tiny 8080 routine and its 8086 translation side by side:
; 8080                     ; 8086
LXI  H, buffer             mov  bx, offset buffer   ; HL becomes BX
MOV  A, M                  mov  al, [bx]            ; A becomes AL
INX  H                     inc  bx
ADD  M                     add  al, [bx]
Now some of the "weird" things about x86 suddenly make sense:
- AX is the accumulator because 8080's A became AL. That's why MUL, DIV, IN, and OUT insist on using it, and why many instructions have shorter encodings when they use AL/AX.
- BX is the base register because the 8080's memory pointer HL became BX. That's why, in 16-bit code, BX is the only one of AX, BX, CX, DX that can point at memory.
- CX is the count register (used by LOOP, REP, and shifts) and DX is the data register (used for I/O port numbers and the high half of 32-bit results).
- The 8080's flags byte became the low byte of the 8086's FLAGS register, and the instructions LAHF and SAHF exist just to move that 8080-shaped byte in and out of AH.
Have you ever wondered why the 8086 numbers its registers in the order AX, CX, DX, BX (0, 1, 2, 3) inside instruction encodings, instead of the obvious A, B, C, D? It follows the 8080's order of register pairs: BC, DE, HL. Once A is placed first, BC becomes CX, DE becomes DX, and HL becomes BX.
And what does the "X" mean? According to Morse himself, nothing special. It was simply an arbitrary letter combining the "H" and "L" halves into one 16-bit register (as told to Vladimir Keleshev).
Segmentation: Reaching 1 MB with 16-bit Registers
The second big requirement was memory. Intel wanted 1 MB of address space, and that needs 20 address bits. But the 8086's registers were only 16 bits wide.
Morse's solution was segmentation. The chip has four segment registers (CS, DS, SS, and ES), and every memory access combines a segment with a 16-bit offset:
$$ \text{address} = \text{segment} \times 16 + \text{offset} $$
Multiplying by 16 is just a shift of 4 bits to the left. For example, if we want to write to pixel (160, 100) in VGA mode 13h, which lives at segment A000h:
mov  ax, 0A000h
mov  es, ax                       ; segment = A000h
mov  di, 320*100 + 160            ; offset  = 7DA0h
mov  byte ptr es:[di], 15         ; physical address = A0000h + 7DA0h = A7DA0h
Why 16 and not something bigger, like 256? Morse explained that with 8 bits of shift, "segments would be forced to start on 256-byte boundaries, resulting in excessive memory fragmentation."
Segmentation was cheap (a small adder in the chip) and it worked very well with the source-compatibility goal: an 8080 program expected a 64 KB world, so you could give it one segment and it would run unchanged, wherever in memory that segment happened to be.
But it also created a rule that haunted every DOS programmer for the next 15 years:
That rule is why C compilers for DOS had near, far, and huge pointers, and memory models with names like tiny, small, compact, and large. It's also why mode 13h is so beloved: 320 × 200 = 64,000 bytes, which fits in one segment!
Operation Crush and the 8088
The 8086 was not an instant hit. Motorola's 68000 and Zilog's Z8000 were more elegant 16-bit designs, and many engineers preferred them.
Intel's response was a sales campaign called Operation Crush, launched in a meeting in December 1979. Instead of selling the 8086 on raw specs, Intel sold it as a complete solution: development tools, support chips, documentation, and support. The goal was 2,000 "design wins" (products using the chip) in one year. They got nearly 2,500.
One of them was a small project inside IBM in Boca Raton.
A year after the 8086, Intel had released the 8088 (June 1, 1979). Internally it's the same 16-bit processor, but with an 8-bit external data bus. Every 16-bit memory access takes two bus cycles, so it's slower. But an 8-bit bus meant you could build the computer with cheap, plentiful support chips designed for the 8085. Intel also offered IBM a better price and could supply more units.
The IBM PC was launched on August 12, 1981, with an 8088 running at 4.77 MHz. That odd number comes from television: the PC used a 14.31818 MHz crystal (four times the NTSC color carrier, which the CGA video card needed), divided by 3.
IBM made one more decision that shaped the whole industry: it required a second source for the CPU, so it would never depend on a single supplier. That led to a 10-year technology exchange agreement between Intel and AMD, first signed in October 1981 and formally executed in February 1982. Keep that agreement in mind, because it comes back with the 386.
The famous "640 KB limit" is not a limit of the CPU. The 8088 could address 1 MB. It was IBM who placed video memory at address A0000h (that's 640 KB) and the BIOS ROM at the top of memory, leaving 640 KB of conventional memory for DOS and its programs.
The "temporary" 8086 family was now inside the machine that would define personal computing. From this point on, every new Intel chip had to run software written for the IBM PC. Compatibility was no longer a nice-to-have.
The 286: Protection Nobody Could Use
The 80286 was released on February 1, 1982, with 134,000 transistors. IBM used it in the PC/AT in 1984, running at 6 MHz.
The 286 was designed for multitasking operating systems. Its new protected mode changed what a segment register means: instead of holding a paragraph number, it holds a selector, an index into a table of descriptors. Each descriptor says where a segment starts (anywhere in 16 MB of memory), how big it is, and who is allowed to use it. The chip checks every memory access against those rules, and runs code in one of four privilege "rings."
On paper, this was fantastic. In practice, it had three problems:
- Segments were still limited to 64 KB.
- DOS programs routinely did arithmetic on segment values (adding 1 to a segment means "16 bytes further"). In protected mode, that produces a random selector and a crash.
- And the biggest one: once you switched to protected mode, you couldn't switch back.
Entering protected mode was as simple as setting one bit:
smsw ax          ; read the Machine Status Word
or   ax, 1       ; set the PE (Protection Enable) bit
lmsw ax          ; ...and there's no instruction to undo this
But DOS and the BIOS only worked in real mode. So how did the PC/AT get back? IBM built a hack into the motherboard: the program wrote a "shutdown code" into the CMOS memory, then asked the keyboard controller to pulse the CPU's reset line. The CPU rebooted, the BIOS noticed the shutdown code, and jumped back into the program, now in real mode. It worked, but it was painfully slow.
Bill Gates famously called the 286 "brain-damaged," mainly because it couldn't run several DOS programs side by side under a protected-mode operating system. Most 286 machines spent their lives running DOS in real mode, as a very fast 8086.
The A20 Gate
The 286 created another, stranger problem. On the 8086, the highest address you can form is FFFF:FFFF, which is 10FFEFh. That needs 21 bits, but the 8086 only has 20 address lines, so the top bit is lost and the address wraps around to the bottom of memory.
Some software depended on that wraparound. DOS's CP/M-style CALL 5 entry point relied on it to reach code at physical address C0h, and programs built with IBM/Microsoft Pascal used it as a space-saving trick. The 286 has 24 address lines, so it does not wrap, and those programs broke.
IBM's fix was to put a logic gate on address line 20 (A20), controlled by... a spare pin on the 8042 keyboard controller. With the gate closed, the PC/AT wraps at 1 MB like an 8086. With it open, real-mode code can reach the High Memory Area: 65,520 bytes just above 1 MB, which is where DOS=HIGH loads DOS.
This hack lived much longer than anyone expected:
A20M# pin to the CPU itself, and according to Intel's manuals, Intel only stopped supporting the A20 gate with the Haswell processors (2013). Source.
                        The 286 also had an undocumented instruction called LOADALL that could load the CPU's hidden segment caches directly, which tools like HIMEM.SYS used to reach extended memory without the slow reset trip. Hidden segment caches will come back very soon.
The 386: Intel Goes Alone
The 80386 was introduced as samples in October 1985, with mass production starting in June 1986. It had 275,000 transistors, and its chief architect was John Crawford (Pat Gelsinger, years later Intel's CEO, also worked on the project).
The 386 fixed the 286's problems one by one:
- 32-bit registers: EAX, EBX, ECX... (the "E" means extended), with AX and AL still living inside them.
- 4 GB segments: set every segment to start at 0 with a 4 GB limit and segmentation effectively disappears. This "flat model" is what DOS extenders like DOS/4GW (used by Doom) gave to C programmers.
- Paging: memory split into 4 KB pages with a two-level page table, which made real virtual memory possible.
- Virtual 8086 mode: a protected-mode task that behaves like an 8086. This is how EMM386 and Windows ran DOS programs safely, each believing it owned the machine.
- A way back: clearing the PE bit in CR0 returns to real mode. No keyboard controller needed!
mov  eax, cr0
and  al, 0FEh    ; clear PE
mov  cr0, eax    ; back in real mode, no reset required
Combining the way back with those hidden segment caches gave demo coders a favorite trick: unreal mode. You enter protected mode, load a segment register with a 4 GB limit, and return to real mode without reloading it. The CPU keeps using the cached 4 GB limit, so your real-mode program (with DOS still working!) can read and write all of memory using 32-bit offsets.
How did 32 bits fit into an instruction set designed for 16? Intel didn't add new opcodes for 32-bit operations. Instead, it added a bit to each code segment that sets the default size, plus two prefix bytes (66h for operand size and 67h for address size) that flip it for a single instruction. That's why a DOS program running in real mode on a 386 can still use EAX: the assembler simply adds a 66h prefix in front of the instruction.
The Business Decision
The 386's biggest story was not technical. Intel decided that the 386 would be single-source. As early as 1984, Intel had decided to stop cooperating with AMD, and it delayed and eventually refused to hand over the 386's technical details. AMD invoked arbitration in 1987, Intel cancelled the 1982 agreement, and the fight went on for years. AMD released its own Am386 in March 1991 (and sold one million of them by October of that year), and in 1994 the Supreme Court of California sided with AMD.
Then something happened that would have been unthinkable a few years before: IBM was not first. The Compaq Deskpro 386 shipped in September 1986, the first time a fundamental part of the IBM PC standard was moved forward by a company other than IBM.
And one more fun detail: some early 386 chips had a bug in 32-bit multiplication. Intel marked the affected chips with "16 BIT S/W ONLY", which was fine at the time because almost all software was still 16-bit anyway!
The 486: Same Instructions, New Engine
The 486 was announced at Spring Comdex on April 10, 1989, and it was the first x86 chip with more than one million transistors (about 1.2 million).
Here's the interesting part: the 486 added almost nothing to the architecture. A few instructions, like BSWAP, XADD, and CMPXCHG, and some control bits. What changed was the engine underneath:
- An 8 KB on-chip cache (16 KB on the later DX4)
- The floating-point unit integrated on the same chip
- A tightly pipelined five-stage design, where simple instructions finally finished in a single clock
Intel kept spinning variants: the 486SX (September 1991) with the FPU disabled, the clock-doubled DX2 (March 1992) that ran the core twice as fast as the motherboard, and the clock-tripled DX4 (March 1994).
For assembly programmers, the pipeline changed the rules of optimization. On the 8086, every instruction ran through microcode, and the "clever" complex instructions were often the fastest way to do things. On the 486, simple instructions became fast, and the old clever ones became the slow ones. The classic example is LOOP:
On an 8086, LOOP was the fast way to write a loop. On a 486, it's almost twice as slow as the "naive" version. If you read Michael Abrash's Graphics Programming Black Book, you'll see this shift everywhere: forget the microcoded tricks, use simple instructions, and keep your data inside the cache.
And Then It Got a Name
So why isn't the next chip called the 586? Because in 1991 Intel lost a trademark dispute over the name "386," when a judge ruled that a number was generic and could not be trademarked. AMD could call its chips "386" and "486" too.
Intel hired a branding agency and came up with a name instead of a number. The Pentium (from the Greek word for "five") was introduced on March 22, 1993. A few years later it would get those famous "with MMX technology" stickers, but that's another story.
Conclusion
Hopefully, by now, you can look at an x86 instruction set reference and see it as a geological record. Every layer was laid down by a specific event:
The pattern is always the same. A chip is designed quickly, often as a stopgap, with one very practical goal in mind. Software starts to depend on its exact behavior (including its accidents). And from that moment on, every future chip has to carry that behavior forward, emulate it, or work around it with a hack.
That's the real lesson of x86 history: the architecture wasn't designed, it accumulated. And once you know the story, the quirks stop being things you memorize and start being things you can explain.
If you're curious to dig deeper, Stephen Morse's "Intel Microprocessors: 8008 to 8086" is a great read straight from the architect, and Ken Shirriff's blog has amazing die-level reverse engineering of the 8086.
And that's it for our trip from a calculator chip to the 486. If you have any suggestions for this article, you can yell at me on Twitter. Also, remember to visit the courses page to access my lectures on retro programming.
See you inside!

articles.title: Hacker Pleads Guilty to Leak of Grand Theft Auto VI Footage
articles.body:
Hacker Pleads Guilty to Leak of Grand Theft Auto VI Footage (therecord.media) 35
			
		 	
				Artion Kurtaj, the British hacker responsible for leaking early footage of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022, pleaded guilty Monday to six offenses stemming from cyberattacks against Rockstar Games, Uber and Revolut. The 21-year-old, who was previously deemed unfit to stand trial due to severe autism, carried out the hacking spree "using a mobile phone and an Amazon Fire Stick connected to a hotel room television," reports The Record, "despite bail restrictions limiting his access to the internet." From the report:  Now 21, he admitted six offenses at Woolwich Crown Court on Monday, four under the Computer Misuse Act, one of fraud and one of possession of a mobile phone in prison, and is due to be sentenced next week. Kurtaj "used sophisticated hacking techniques to carry out a sustained campaign of cyberattacks, causing serious disruption to major international business and putting sensitive information at risk," said specialist prosecutor Robert Hutchinson.
"The defendant was involved in a hacking group responsible for attacks which caused millions of dollars in losses. His offending was calculated and, even after being charged with serious offenses, he continued to target organizations, demonstrating a persistent disregard for the harm he was causing and the law. This was an exceptionally complex and challenging case, but despite his efforts to conceal his identity online, our specialist prosecutors were able to work closely with the City of London Police and international law enforcement partners to build a strong case that exposed his actions and resulted in his guilty pleas," said Hutchinson.

articles.title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster
articles.body:
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.
China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks.
Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff.
The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.”
Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely.
Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue.
In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change.
Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.
Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China.
That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch.
If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share.

articles.title: Nvidia says it doesn’t plan to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.body:
Despite Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang’s recent offer to return to the chip company he helped build from the ground up, the company is not looking to take him back.
During the company’s earnings call on Tuesday, Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones told listeners that Huang’s return was not something that company leadership was considering.
“On November 12, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms,” Jones said, “Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”
On Tuesday, Huang had posted on X that since he left the company, he has “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and added that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang resigned last week in dramatic fashion following revelations of a number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. That woman, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, has maintained close ties to the former Nvidia CEO for years. Critics worry that the relationship may have influenced Nvidia’s dealings with China, and U.S. intelligence officials have expressed suspicions that she works for China’s Ministry of State Security.
The development has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry at a moment when the future of the AI business, in which Nvidia plays a pivotal role, hangs in the balance. It has also spurred investigations, including an independent investigation into Huang’s activities by Nvidia’s board and an SEC probe into Nvidia. Huang has been replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress, who is also the chipmaker’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, while the board searches for a permanent replacement. Jones added Tuesday that the company was looking at both internal and external candidates.

articles.title: Highly Classified NSA Network Goes Down
articles.body:
Highly Classified NSA Network Goes Down (cnn.com) 65
			
		 	
				"CNN and other outlets are reporting that a classified network at the NSA is down," writes longtime Slashdot reader frdmfghtr. "This follows a week of major outages at Microsoft, the FAA, and JPMorgan Chase." From a report:  The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said.
"We see no evidence that this was a cyberattack," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Tuesday on Newsmax. "There is no crisis, or anything like that, for Americans to be worried about." [...] The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official.  The NSA released a statement addressing the network issues: "The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events."

articles.title: Nvidia’s Q3 earnings hit the mark, without mentioning the whole Jensen Huang thing
articles.body:
Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress announced the company’s Q3 earnings on Tuesday, without initially mentioning former CEO Jensen Huang or the details of his departure, or possible attempt at a return. On the earnings call accompanying the release, board chair Harvey Jones kicked things off by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO,” and that “we will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation,” before Kress started with her comments on the results.
Nvidia’s Q3 earnings hit the mark, without mentioning the whole Jensen Huang thing
Nvidia’s Q3 revenue has more than doubled, with income from data centers up 110 percent from last year, to $107.6 billion.
As it predicted in the last financial update, Nvidia is now on the list of companies that have pulled in over $100 billion in a single quarter, with revenues of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent from the same period last year and higher than its expectation of $108 billion. This quarter’s figures include data center revenues of $107.6 billion, which were up 110 percent, and edge computing (which includes the consumer gaming PC business and devices like the new RTX Spark laptops) revenue of $8.2 billion, up 42 percent.
The company reported $65.3 billion in profit, a new record.
“Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer of NVIDIA. “Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.”
In the fourth quarter, Nvidia expects revenues of $130 billion.
Update, November 17th: Added comments from Nvidia’s earnings call.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return As Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return As Nvidia CEO (npr.org) 62
			
		 	
				In a post on X today, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he would be "honored" to return to the company if its board gives the approval. "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," he says. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
Huang resigned from the company last week after acknowledging multiple affairs, including one with a women whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. NPR reports:  His comments come as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen."
"We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.  The report notes that Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors before three congressional committees on December 1 and 2.

articles.title: Nvidia clarifies when it will — and won’t —keep financing neoclouds
articles.body:
One reason 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition over the weekend calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang is that he wasn’t just championing the AI boom. He was using Nvidia’s enormous profits to help finance it.
And Nvidia has a lot of money to spend. The company reported on Tuesday net income of $64.9 billion for the third quarter, which was up from $59.7 billion the prior quarter.
But Nvidia’s continued success depends on having enough customers building and expanding data centers to keep buying its AI chips and systems. Under Huang, the company aggressively invested in AI startups and neoclouds and, more recently, began guaranteeing massive loans to finance new data centers. The biggest deal yet was the $105 billion backstop for OpenAI’s PORTS-Pike data center campus in Ohio, announced in August. In exchange for that loan guarantee, OpenAI promised that the campus would exclusively use Nvidia’s equipment, the company said.
Huang’s abrupt departure last week raised questions about whether Nvidia would continue bankrolling its customers at the same pace. There were reports that CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO, had tried to push back on Huang’s increasingly ambitious dealmaking. She reportedly reduced the backstop guarantee for the OpenAI project from $250 billion down to $105 billion.
Under Kress, Nvidia clarified in its quarterly CFO commentary that guaranteeing a loan doesn’t mean the company is providing the financing itself. The guarantee only takes effect once the customer has secured the financing needed to build the facility and install Nvidia’s products. If the project fails to meet those conditions, the guarantee “doesn’t exist” she said.
“There is the raising of capital that they may need through equity and or debt, in order to build out any of the buildings, get them ready for use, but also the ability to procure the compute, install the compute, and get ready. What we are indicating in our statement there is that is when our guarantee starts. So if all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore,” Kress said to analysts on Tuesday during the quarterly conference call.
She pointed to OpenAI PORTS-Pike campus as an example of where such terms apply. When asked, she also said this wasn’t a change in policy, but simply a clarification of existing terms. However, these disclosures have never been public before.
Kress also made clear that Nvidia wasn’t bailing on all the ways it was financing the AI boom, especially new data centers. But, she said, Nvidia was going to be far more selective in the future.
“The availability of land, power, shell is such a critical part of the whole structure in terms of building out those data centers. So they may need the assistance. That’s a great asset for anyone to hold. So we will look at that as probably one of our top priorities,” she said. At the same time, she insisted that Nvidia was “taking a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing.”
One of the ongoing criticisms Huang faced was his love of circular deals: invest in his customers so they would turn around and buy his products. Kress is now trying to strike a delicate balance. She isn’t saying she will pull the rug out from under Nvidia’s customers. After all, the company’s investments undoubtedly spurred the AI boom that has been so lucrative for Nvidia. But she’s also signaling that the days of Huang’s freewheeling dealmaking may be over.

articles.title: Microsoft AI: Seven new world-class models at scalable price-performance
articles.body:
MAI Licensed Weights: Frontier performance you control
At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability.
But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you run agents 24-7 doing real engineering work.
That’s why today we’re releasing a family of seven new world class models at a truly exceptional price-performance:
Here’s the lineup:
Security, alignment and containment are the most important priorities for agent development in 2027 and beyond. That’s our top priority. We need to run monitoring and control agents defending and patching live production systems 24-7. That’s why MAI Cyber 2 Flash was designed to deliver frontier intelligence at a fraction of the cost.
Built with Microsoft’s decades of proprietary data and world class security expertise, our models help defenders stay safe in this new era where attackers have cheap and abundant offensive tools.
MAI Cyber 2 Flash builds on earlier MAI Cyber models that defenders already rely on. MAI Cyber accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, and 90% of scans that started with MAI continued to use it. Our latest model is now priced 86% lower on output tokens than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, giving existing MDASH customers a stronger model at a lower price.
MAI Code 2 is built for the best price-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the price.
We’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work.
MAI Code 2 also been tuned to generate great dashboards and visualizations. In a blind, side-by-side evaluation of frontend work, developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. Try MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot today. Read more here.
MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume, everyday tasks like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. It performs comparably to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the price, respectively, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas). It’s available in GitHub Copilot and in a limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry.
MAI Image 2.7 is the best image editing model in the world, taking the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. At text-to-image generation, our model is ranked #4, making us the second-best lab. And MAI Image 2.7 Flash brings world class image generation for high-volume scenarios at ~$10 per 1,000 images. Both are available in Microsoft Foundry here.
MAI Realtime 1 is our first live speech-to-speech model, designed for natural, low-latency conversations. In our evaluations, it outperformed GPT-Realtime 2.1 across external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. It’s priced for enterprise-scale use, starting at a budget-saving price of $0.01 per audio minute. You can try it out in MAI Labs and register your interest here.
Dragon Copilot Transcribe, built on MAI Transcribe 2, is now live in Dragon Copilot, powering 100% of doctor–patient conversation transcriptions. It covers 10 million encounters a month, halves error rates in multilingual workflows, and is in the hands of a third of US physicians.
Decision 1.1 provides model routing integrated right into your applications so that the bigger, pricier models are only used when you really need them. On the AA Decision Index Microsoft is ahead of Jev, Google and OpenAI, while being faster and cheaper. Used by 4,000 customers, it’s 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol.
We’ve heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model.
And if you build on open weights, can you really trust where they came from, or how they’ll behave when you use one as the foundation for your most valuable IP and data?
We heard you. We started with Custom Models. AT&T developed an MAI custom model for 5G network operation analytics and it outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at 50x cheaper cost. On complex scenarios, they found that Code 2 delivered frontier-level performance at a significantly lower price than alternatives.
Today, we’re taking a big step forward with MAI Licensed Weights: models under your control.
Take a frontier MAI model, customize it using your proprietary data if you want to. Then run it securely in your own Azure environment.
You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents.
So that’s MAI, a family of world class models with exceptional price performance: the world’s best image editing model; the world’s best transcription model; frontier cyber defense at 2% of the cost; and world class everyday coding models at a price you can scale.
And crucially all of it with Your IQ. Your agents. Your weights. All under your control.
This is Frontier Intelligence you can trust, from the company you can trust.

articles.title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
articles.body:
Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage.
For eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work.

News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat
Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff
Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found.
In the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Two legal AI announcements this month, Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and a court-filing redaction agent Cooley is developing with Google Cloud, place a lawyer at a comparable review step, and neither reports a measure of it.
What the Harvard data measured
How much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira issues, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data.
The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months.
The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI.
The current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. Her website lists coverage links to The Wall Street Journal and The Economist, and legal trade press picked it up this month, including an Oct. 12 eDiscovery Today post by Doug Austin that relayed an Ars Technica report.
Drafts went up and finished issues did not
With that provenance in view, the coding results are large. Lines of code added rose by 1,494 per worker-month against a baseline of 5,017, about 30 percent. Commits rose 20 percent, and pull requests, the bundles of code submitted for review, rose 23 percent. The authors note that these estimates capture the added effect of agents at firms that already had AI coding assistants, not the effect of AI from a standing start.
Output is where the gain stops. The paper counts finished work as Jira issues resolved, and an issue counts as complete when its code is deployed to production. Agents moved that measure by 0.12 issues per worker-month on a 3.67 baseline, with a standard error of 0.17. That result is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the 95 percent confidence interval rules out an increase above about 12 percent of the baseline, well short of the 30 percent rise in code written.
The authors tested the obvious escape route. If engineers had shifted to larger tasks, a flat issue count would understate real output. So the researchers labeled a 0.5 percent sample of issues by size with GPT-4o and extended those labels to every issue with a text-embedding model. They found no shift in average issue size, and pull requests did not grow larger either, which the authors use to set aside the simplest explanation for what happened in review.
Where the shortfall shows up: the review queue
The paper locates the shortfall in code review. The time from pull request submission to merge rose 3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline, a 49 percent increase. The share of pull requests receiving a formal change request increased by about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 13 percent, nearly doubling, and review comments per pull request rose 35 percent. The share of workers doing any code review rose 14 percent from a base of about 29 percent, while the share writing code showed no measurable change.
AI review tools did not remove the bottleneck. By March 2026, nearly 80 percent of the firms had used one, yet AI generated only 23.3 percent of review comments, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests received even one AI comment. The authors write that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt such tools. The paper’s interviews show what that looks like on a team: a junior software engineer described a project where only one senior engineer could approve changes and could review the interviewee’s code only once a week. “After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks,” the engineer said, in a quote the authors say they lightly edited for clarity.
That account fits the model the authors use to explain their numbers, which has two channels. In the first, faster drafting sends more code to a fixed pool of reviewers, a problem that moving labor into review can largely relieve. In the second, the rise in change requests and comments, which faster drafting alone does not explain, reads through the model as a sign of lower-quality drafts. That problem, the authors say, would require better technology. Anyone buying an agent should care which channel dominates, because the two call for different spending.
Employment did not move either
Nor did the coding gains show up as job cuts. The estimates rule out a decline in overall employment larger than 2.9 percent. A noisier estimate rules out a decline in engineering employment larger than 13.8 percent. The authors caution that these are short-run effects measured in partial equilibrium, which could mask job losses at competing firms, and that the assistant estimate for engineering employment shows upward pre-trends that make it hard to read causally.
Legal AI tools are designed around a similar checkpoint
Those software results arrive as legal AI tools adopt a related design, and the Harvey and Cooley announcements both follow it: automate a first pass, then keep a lawyer at the checkpoint. Harvey’s workflow, co-developed with LexisNexis and announced Oct. 7, is the drafting case. Harvey says the multi-step process of reading the complaint, researching and drafting a motion to dismiss “commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work” and that its tool produces the research and a first draft “in a matter of hours.” The announcement describes “human checkpoints at the moments where a lawyer’s judgment matters most,” but it does not state how long lawyers spend at those checkpoints or how long it takes to reach a motion ready to file.
Cooley’s Oct. 8 announcement applies the same posture to a different task, since its agent recommends redactions rather than drafting arguments. Cooley says the agent is still being developed and that attorneys make all redaction determinations before a filing goes to the court, which puts the human checkpoint at the last step before submission. As ComplexDiscovery reported Oct. 10, the announcement carries no error rate.
For a motion filed in federal court, the checkpoint is a legal duty rather than a design choice. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b), an attorney presenting a motion certifies several things about it to the best of the attorney’s knowledge, information and belief, “formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.” Its legal contentions must be “warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing new law.” Its factual contentions must have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, be likely to have it after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery. A first draft can arrive in hours, but that inquiry stays with the attorney, and the software evidence raises the possibility that review could absorb some of the drafting savings.
The paper’s method carries a second lesson, this one for information governance teams. The researchers identified agent use partly from traces inside the firms’ own systems, including bot accounts tied to AI tools and signatures such as “Co-authored-by” lines in commit messages and pull request descriptions. AI authorship can leave its own metadata trail in collaboration systems. That trail is a record that a retention schedule and a legal hold may need to reach.
None of this means legal work will behave like software, and the limits of the comparison matter. Document review is not code review, a production is not a pull request, and Chen and Stratton studied no legal work. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, revised in September 2026, reports a similar falloff using data on over 500,000 GitHub developers. Its authors, Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, found a 240 percent cumulative rise in commits from autonomous agents shrinking to 30 percent for actual releases. That paper carries its own disclosure: Demirer and Musolff each previously held a postdoctoral research position at Microsoft, which owns GitHub, and each now works as a paid research consultant for the company. Two software studies point to a pattern in software, not a finding about law firms.
Document review offers a partial precedent
Discovery practitioners have argued a version of this question before, and Austin’s post draws that comparison. He wrote that discovery has seen a similar debate over generative AI review, with some practitioners saying manual validation offsets the gains and others, including him, saying statistical sampling of the kind used in predictive coding is enough. For coding agents, though, he wrote that the extra review time may be warranted, since code that is 90 percent correct can still fail to run.
His comparison suggests a useful split between two kinds of legal output. Population-level work such as first-pass relevance review can be validated by sampling. A single filing is different, because its citations, factual assertions and sensitive data generally need direct examination when one fabricated citation or one missed Social Security number is the failure. Buyers can turn that split into a test. Ask a vendor which kind of output its agent produces, then ask for the downstream measure rather than the drafting one: hours from upload to an approved work product, the share of drafts a reviewing attorney sent back and reviewer time per matter. Budget review capacity before scaling drafting volume, and log what reviewers change, because that log shows whether the bottleneck is volume or quality.
Read the paper’s limits as closely as its findings
Those questions apply to the paper’s own sourcing, too. The data partner has a commercial interest in the subject, and the relationship runs deeper than a data license. Jellyfish describes itself as an “AI Impact Platform,” and the authors have published on its blog: a Sept. 25, 2025, post by Chen and Stratton described itself as “part of our ongoing work with Jellyfish.” The paper thanks the Jellyfish team “for their partnership” and states that Jellyfish reviewed the manuscript only to check for proprietary disclosure, not for scientific content, and that the conclusions are the authors’. Its funders were the Stripe Economics of AI Fellowship, a Harvard Kennedy School program on wealth distribution and the Schmidt Sciences AI at Work Program.
Jellyfish has also promoted an earlier version of the work. A Jan. 28 post on its blog by Nicholas Arcolano called it “a preliminary version of a new paper from our collaborators at Harvard Economics, Fiona Chen and James Stratton,” based on 100,000 software engineers across 500 companies. That post, and a March 17 Jellyfish press release after it, reported that AI was making coding faster and that “code quality doesn’t seem to be suffering.” The August version, built on a larger sample running through March 2026, reads the near-doubling in change requests through its model as a possible sign of lower draft quality. The two descriptions rest on different versions and samples, so they need not conflict, but a reader relying on Jellyfish’s summary would miss the quality question the current paper raises.
The paper also carries small internal inconsistencies that do not touch the headline agent estimates. Its introduction rounds the sample to about 700 firms and 700,000 workers, and its main text describes 17 interviews where an appendix describes 21. Other limits are structural rather than clerical: the underlying data are proprietary, and use of AI tools through individual licenses goes unrecorded.
None of those caveats overturns the central result, though the March 2026 data cutoff means a revision could move the figures. What the paper offers is a standard the two legal announcements discussed here do not meet: named authors, a disclosed method, a confidence interval and a measured checkpoint. If an agent cuts 40 hours of research and drafting to a few, how many of those hours reappear on the desk of the lawyer who signs the motion?

- Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production (Fiona Chen and James Stratton, Harvard University)
- Fiona Chen (Fiona Chen)
- James Stratton | Department of Economics (Harvard University Department of Economics)
- Writing Code vs. Shipping Code: Productivity Effects Across Generations of AI Coding Tools (National Bureau of Economic Research)
- Rule 11. Signing Pleadings, Motions, and Other Papers; Representations to the Court; Sanctions (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School)

- Cooley Collaborates With Google Cloud to Develop AI Agent for Complex Litigation (Cooley)
- Jellyfish Reveals AI’s Real Impact on Engineering Teams with Industry’s Largest Ongoing Benchmark Study (Jellyfish)
- New Research from Harvard & Jellyfish: AI Is Making Developers Faster. So Where’s the Business Impact? (Jellyfish)
- Does AI Assistance Mean Engineers Are Doing Less Coding Work? Maybe Not. (Jellyfish)
- AI Coding Agents Productivity Gains Offset by Human Review (eDiscovery Today)

Document review is not code review, a production is not a pull request, and Chen and Stratton studied no legal work. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, revised in September 2026, reports a similar falloff using data on over 500,000 GitHub developers. Its authors, Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, found a 240 percent cumulative rise in commits from autonomous agents shrinking to 30 percent for actual releases. That paper carries its own disclosure: Demirer and Musolff each previously held a postdoctoral research position at Microsoft, which owns GitHub, and each now works as a paid research consultant for the company. Two software studies point to a pattern in software, not a finding about law firms.
Document review offers a partial precedent
Discovery practitioners have argued a version of this question before, and Austin’s post draws that comparison. He wrote that discovery has seen a similar debate over generative AI review, with some practitioners saying manual validation offsets the gains and others, including him, saying statistical sampling of the kind used in predictive coding is enough. For coding agents, though, he wrote that the extra review time may be warranted, since code that is 90 percent correct can still fail to run.
His comparison suggests a useful split between two kinds of legal output. Population-level work such as first-pass relevance review can be validated by sampling. A single filing is different, because its citations, factual assertions and sensitive data generally need direct examination when one fabricated citation or one missed Social Security number is the failure. Buyers can turn that split into a test. Ask a vendor which kind of output its agent produces, then ask for the downstream measure rather than the drafting one: hours from upload to an approved work product, the share of drafts a reviewing attorney sent back and reviewer time per matter. Budget review capacity before scaling drafting volume, and log what reviewers change, because that log shows whether the bottleneck is volume or quality.
Read the paper’s limits as closely as its findings
Those questions apply to the paper’s own sourcing, too. The data partner has a commercial interest in the subject, and the relationship runs deeper than a data license. Jellyfish describes itself as an “AI Impact Platform,” and the authors have published on its blog: a Sept. 25, 2025, post by Chen and Stratton described itself as “part of our ongoing work with Jellyfish.” The paper thanks the Jellyfish team “for their partnership” and states that Jellyfish reviewed the manuscript only to check for proprietary disclosure, not for scientific content, and that the conclusions are the authors’. Its funders were the Stripe Economics of AI Fellowship, a Harvard Kennedy School program on wealth distribution and the Schmidt Sciences AI at Work Program.
Jellyfish has also promoted an earlier version of the work. A Jan. 28 post on its blog by Nicholas Arcolano called it “a preliminary version of a new paper from our collaborators at Harvard Economics, Fiona Chen and James Stratton,” based on 100,000 software engineers across 500 companies. That post, and a March 17 Jellyfish press release after it, reported that AI was making coding faster and that “code quality doesn’t seem to be suffering.” The August version, built on a larger sample running through March 2026, reads the near-doubling in change requests through its model as a possible sign of lower draft quality. The two descriptions rest on different versions and samples, so they need not conflict, but a reader relying on Jellyfish’s summary would miss the quality question the current paper raises.
The paper also carries small internal inconsistencies that do not touch the headline agent estimates. Its introduction rounds the sample to about 700 firms and 700,000 workers, and its main text describes 17 interviews where an appendix describes 21. Other limits are structural rather than clerical: the underlying data are proprietary, and use of AI tools through individual licenses goes unrecorded.
None of those caveats overturns the central result, though the March 2026 data cutoff means a revision could move the figures. What the paper offers is a standard the two legal announcements discussed here do not meet: named authors, a disclosed method, a confidence interval and a measured checkpoint. If an agent cuts 40 hours of research and drafting to a few, how many of those hours reappear on the desk of the lawyer who signs the motion?
