articles.title: China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly
articles.body:
Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years. Many of those are made in the U.S., but they’re largely dependent on China for key ingredients, including graphite.
Graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge. Chinese companies control about three-quarters of the graphite anode supply chain and 97% of synthetic (human-made) graphite anode production, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. One five-year-old startup, Molten Industries, is working to break that dominance.
Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. The plant is will pave the way for U.S.-made graphite to win a share of the market.
“The new plant will be producing graphite that’s at cost parity with China plus tariffs,” Caleb Boyd, co-founder and CTO of Molten Industries, told TechCrunch. In other words, once U.S. import taxes are added to Chinese graphite, Molten’s price would match it. He said future plants should match China’s cost even without tariffs, which he called a built-in advantage of the technology.
Molten’s Oakland plant will make about 300 metric tons of graphite annually, which is enough for 300 megawatt-hours of batteries. That’s enough for about 4,300 EVs. The bulk of the output will go to undisclosed customers that are testing it in their battery cells.
The next facility, which Molten has yet to announce, will take the same template used in the Oakland plant and replicate it several times over, said Boyd.
The startup’s technology began in a Silicon Valley garage. It uses electrical resistive heating, which passes electricity through a material to heat it, to split methane (the main ingredient in natural gas) into pure carbon and hydrogen. “You can think of it almost like a massive toaster,” Boyd said. The company says the system uses three times less electricity than existing methods, and it runs on natural gas, which is cheap and plentiful in the U.S.
“We think it’s very hard to compete with China if you’re just copying their processes and trying to compete on cost,” said Kevin Bush, who co-founded Molten Industries with Boyd and is the company’s CEO. “So we are using a resource in the United States that’s abundant in natural gas, and we’ve brought some innovation to actually be able to drive down the cost of graphite production globally.”
Here’s how the chemistry works: When methane (CH4) is heated without oxygen, each molecule breaks into one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. The hydrogen atoms pair up into hydrogen gas (H2), which Molten sells at market prices to a customer next door. The carbon is then processed to meet battery makers’ requirements.
The basic idea of using heat to separate methane has been around for over a century, but early attempts to commercialize it ran into trouble. Carbon built up and clogged the reactor, and Boyd said no company before Molten had been able to produce high-quality graphite this way.
Solving that problem changed the company’s direction. Boyd and Bush — both materials science PhDs from Stanford — originally set out to make clean hydrogen from natural gas. Most hydrogen today comes from steam reforming, a cheap but polluting process. The two wanted to reap the benefits of a low-cost feedstock like natural gas without the pollution, and they expected to sell the leftover carbon as a byproduct.
But as they experimented with ways to keep the reactor clean, “we actually started making this really high quality graphite,” Boyd said, which “changed the entire economics of what we were doing.” Molten went from a hydrogen company that happened to sell graphite to a battery-grade graphite company that happens to sell hydrogen.
The company says both businesses could bring in billions of dollars. If Molten supplied the entire U.S. battery market, it could also provide about a third of the hydrogen used in the country, the company claims. Other uses for high-quality graphite, like thermal batteries that store energy as heat, could expand both markets further.
The new factory, Boyd said, “is really a milestone, not just for the company, we think, but globally.”

articles.title: Nvidia Rejects Jensen Huang's Offer to Return as CEO
articles.body:
Nvidia Rejects Jensen Huang's Offer to Return as CEO (apnews.com) 73
			
		 	
				Nvidia's board has unanimously rejected former CEO Jensen Huang's offer to return, despite public support from President Trump and prominent Silicon Valley figures. The decision came as Nvidia reported blockbuster third-quarter revenue of $116 billion, double the year-earlier figure. The Associated Press reports:  The embattled company's board of directors "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of Nvidia's quarterly earnings call before yielding to Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who is running the company as a permanent replacement is sought. [...] Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said in a social media post that if the board decided that his return was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and the country, he would be "honored to answer these calls." He acknowledged making "serious mistakes" in his personal life.
The turmoil notwithstanding, Nvidia blew past Wall Street expectations for the third quarter, pulling in $116 billion in revenue, double the level from a year ago. The company also posted net income of $2.70 per share, beating estimates of $2.48 per share. Nvidia stock shot up 5.2% in after-hours trading. Referring to Huang's replacement, Jones said, "We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person."   Nvidia also announced a new board committee overseeing national security and trade compliance amid investigations into alleged AI chip smuggling to China.
Further reading: Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion

articles.title: Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion
articles.body:
Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion (ft.com) 20
			
		 	
				Nvidia stopped separately disclosing its Singapore sales (source paywalled; alternative source) after changing its geographic revenue reporting methodology from customer billing addresses to headquarters locations, obscuring a business that generated $104 billion in external revenue in 2025, up 72% from the previous year. The Financial Times reports that the change has drawn scrutiny amid U.S. investigations into whether Singapore-based Megaspeed helped smuggle Nvidia chips into China. From the report:  "There is now a lot more focus on Nvidia's Singapore business and questions about who its end customers are," said an investor who is investigating Nvidia's dealings in south-east Asia. The Singapore accounts show that the subsidiary booked $117.8 billion of revenue in the 12 months to January 2026, including $13.6 billion of sales to another Nvidia company. Given the nature of the Singapore operation as a global hub, customers it serves are from all over the world. Only a small quantity of the chips Nvidia sells ends up in or goes through Singapore. The Singapore subsidiary generated just $53 million of profit in the year to January 2026, suggesting limited scope for Nvidia to benefit from Singapore's low corporate tax rates.
[...] Singapore's outsized role as a revenue generator for Nvidia used to show up in the company's overall results. In January 2025, the US company reported that Singapore was its second-biggest geographic area by revenue, based on customer billing location. The Singapore office generated $23.7 billion of revenue, behind only the US and representing 18 per cent of global income, based on customers' billing location. The annual accounts said that most of the business was generated by customers using the Singapore office to centralize invoicing and that most of the products were shipped elsewhere, with less than 2 per cent of revenue tied to chips that landed in the city-state.
As recently as July last year, Nvidia reported that the Singapore office accounted for 22 per cent of total revenue. This was around the time Nvidia said it began cutting ties with Megaspeed, following US Department of Commerce investigations into the business. Nvidia then changed its financial reporting methodology and stopped splitting out revenue that went to the Singapore office. Before the 2025 reporting change, Nvidia said in its financial filing that it booked sales based on the billing locations of its customers, but that the end customer's location "may be different than our customer's billing location." It added that "most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant," according to the filings.

articles.title: India’s Humyn Labs raises $47M to feed U.S. robotics companies the data they need
articles.body:
As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies build models that can operate in physical environments.
The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital.
Companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks, but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult. Startups including Mecka AI, XDOF, and MicroAGI are already tackling the problem by collecting real-world data for robotics training. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs aims to compete with them.
Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. The startup collects data across over 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea serving as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal (pictured above, right) said in an interview.
Agarwal, the former CEO of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta (pictured above, left), a former executive at the brewing giant AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN. KGeN has a network of contributors across emerging markets, and that network helps Humyn Labs collect data in people’s homes, the founders told TechCrunch.
Collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal said. He added that Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, interactions with objects, and other details, turning raw recordings into data that AI models can learn from.
“Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem,” Agarwal said.
Humyn Labs says it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, though he declined to name specific customers.
The startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal told TechCrunch, adding that a further $20 million in deals has yet to be finalized.
That growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal said, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said.
Over the last few months, India has emerged as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, with startups including Human Archive and BuildAI tapping into the country’s large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. However, the practice has also raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly when people are recorded inside their homes.
Agarwal said Humyn Labs collects data from people doing their usual work or household chores instead of asking them to perform staged activities. The startup works with local partners to identify collection sites and oversee the process. “The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input,” he stated.
Humyn Labs currently has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, plus a network of local partners across the countries where it collects data, Agarwal said.

articles.title: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
articles.body:
Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
Discussion on Hacker News
While benchmarking Gemini 4 Carbon on one of our private evals, we found something surprising: it spent close to an hour completing tasks that routinely took Opus and Astra only a few minutes:
Turns out we weren't alone in noticing this.
I don't really know how to properly emphasize this. Gemini 4 Carbon is unacceptably slow in real world usage.
Gemini 4 Carbon low: 22m21s
Opus 5.5 high: 9m33s
i really love gemini 4 carbon but its too slow. im losing my mind waiting just to stay focused and learn simple things
dude why is carbon so fucking slow
carbon is nearly unusable because of how slow it is, but people are majorly sleeping on it
To find out why, we traced every step of Carbon's runs and quantified what contributes to the slowness.
The Task
In each task, the agent gets a codebase from just before a bug was fixed, along with a report that describes the bug only by its symptoms. Its job is to diagnose the bug and fix it, without making any unrelated changes.
Much of the task's difficulty comes from engineering judgment rather than raw intelligence: tracing the user's symptoms to the right code path, ruling out rival explanations, putting the fix in the right place, and knowing when to stop.
Slow inference, or more work?
The first (and easiest) factor to separate out was inference speed: queueing at the provider, network latency, prompt processing and generation speed. Together, these set how long each step takes:
Slower inference accounts for part of the gap: 16–30% of Carbon’s extra time compared with Astra, and 45–49% compared with Opus. The rest comes from longer trajectories. Carbon simply does more work per task, as the step counts, tool calls and tokens below show:
Carbon takes about seven times as many steps as Astra, and eleven times as many actions such as reading a file or running a command. It writes seven times as much and, because every step re-sends a longer and longer conversation, it processes more than sixteen times as much input.
Ruling out the obvious
Before looking inside the runs, we checked two simpler explanations.
- The harness. We also ran Carbon inside two other coding agents, opencode and mini-SWE-agent, and saw no meaningful difference.
- Mismatched reasoning levels. Effort settings aren't standardized across providers, so Carbon's "high" may sit closer to the other models' maximum settings, and the fairer comparison might have been Carbon on low. But on low, Carbon often failed to produce a fix at all: it went in circles, re-reading code it had already read instead of making the fix.
Reading the traces
We labelled every step of the Astra and Carbon runs by what it was for, and then counted how many steps went to each kind of work:
Half of Carbon’s steps went into work the ticket never asked for:
- Auditing code beyond the bug. Once it had found the cause, Carbon kept widening its search, checking every related path through the system and auditing code the fix never needed to touch.
- Closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Carbon defended against cases the ticket's facts had already excluded, hardening the code against problems nobody had reported.
In this sample trial, both models identified the cause early, Astra within a minute and Carbon within about six. Astra had its fix written three minutes later; Carbon didn't write any code for another 25 minutes.
Carbon might not have been sure it had the cause (a knowledge gap), or it might have known and kept going anyway (a general habit, learned from training that rewards right answers more than it penalises extra steps). To tell them apart, we re-ran one of the trials in a modified harness that automatically injects the same check-in every five turns: "do you already have enough to make the fix?"
With check-ins, Carbon finished in 28 minutes instead of 37, and the wait between naming the cause and editing shrank from 25 minutes to about 10. This implies that the slowness seems to come from how Carbon behaves, not what it knows.
Carbon's necessary work is also slower
Even within the steps the fix needed, we found some additional low-hanging fruit: Carbon got less done with each step, and it kept re-reading code it had already seen.
Astra made more than two tool calls per step, often reading several files at once — Carbon, on the other hand, made about one, usually reading a single file. Carbon also re-read far more: 39% of the lines it read were ones it had already seen, against 7% for Astra. We estimate that these two "mechanical" inefficiencies account for roughly 25% of Carbon's excess runtime.
Conclusion
On difficult bug-fixing tasks, Carbon took close to an hour where Opus and Astra took minutes. We traced that gap to three sources:
- Slower inference. Each step takes longer, which explains 16–30% of the gap against Astra and about half against Opus.
- Unnecessary work. About half of Carbon's steps went on work the tickets never asked for: auditing code the fix didn't need and closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out.
- Mechanical inefficiencies. Fewer tool calls per step and frequent re-reading slow Carbon down; we estimate that fixing them alone would cut its runtime by roughly a quarter.

Turns out we weren't alone in noticing this.
I don't really know how to properly emphasize this. Gemini 4 Carbon is unacceptably slow in real world usage.
Gemini 4 Carbon low: 22m21s
Opus 5.5 high: 9m33s
i really love gemini 4 carbon but its too slow. im losing my mind waiting just to stay focused and learn simple things
dude why is carbon so fucking slow
carbon is nearly unusable because of how slow it is, but people are majorly sleeping on it
To find out why, we traced every step of Carbon's runs and quantified what contributes to the slowness.
The Task
In each task, the agent gets a codebase from just before a bug was fixed, along with a report that describes the bug only by its symptoms. Its job is to diagnose the bug and fix it, without making any unrelated changes.
Much of the task's difficulty comes from engineering judgment rather than raw intelligence: tracing the user's symptoms to the right code path, ruling out rival explanations, putting the fix in the right place, and knowing when to stop.
Slow inference, or more work?
The first (and easiest) factor to separate out was inference speed: queueing at the provider, network latency, prompt processing and generation speed. Together, these set how long each step takes:
Slower inference accounts for part of the gap: 16–30% of Carbon’s extra time compared with Astra, and 45–49% compared with Opus. The rest comes from longer trajectories. Carbon simply does more work per task, as the step counts, tool calls and tokens below show:
Carbon takes about seven times as many steps as Astra, and eleven times as many actions such as reading a file or running a command. It writes seven times as much and, because every step re-sends a longer and longer conversation, it processes more than sixteen times as much input.
Ruling out the obvious
Before looking inside the runs, we checked two simpler explanations.
- The harness. We also ran Carbon inside two other coding agents, opencode and mini-SWE-agent, and saw no meaningful difference.
- Mismatched reasoning levels. Effort settings aren't standardized across providers, so Carbon's "high" may sit closer to the other models' maximum settings, and the fairer comparison might have been Carbon on low. But on low, Carbon often failed to produce a fix at all: it went in circles, re-reading code it had already read instead of making the fix.
Reading the traces
We labelled every step of the Astra and Carbon runs by what it was for, and then counted how many steps went to each kind of work:
Half of Carbon’s steps went into work the ticket never asked for:
- Auditing code beyond the bug. Once it had found the cause, Carbon kept widening its search, checking every related path through the system and auditing code the fix never needed to touch.
- Closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Carbon defended against cases the ticket's facts had already excluded, hardening the code against problems nobody had reported.
In this sample trial, both models identified the cause early, Astra within a minute and Carbon within about six. Astra had its fix written three minutes later; Carbon didn't write any code for another 25 minutes.
Carbon might not have been sure it had the cause (a knowledge gap), or it might have known and kept going anyway (a general habit, learned from training that rewards right answers more than it penalises extra steps). To tell them apart, we re-ran one of the trials in a modified harness that automatically injects the same check-in every five turns: "do you already have enough to make the fix?"
With check-ins, Carbon finished in 28 minutes instead of 37, and the wait between naming the cause and editing shrank from 25 minutes to about 10. This implies that the slowness seems to come from how Carbon behaves, not what it knows.
Carbon's necessary work is also slower
Even within the steps the fix needed, we found some additional low-hanging fruit: Carbon got less done with each step, and it kept re-reading code it had already seen.
Astra made more than two tool calls per step, often reading several files at once — Carbon, on the other hand, made about one, usually reading a single file. Carbon also re-read far more: 39% of the lines it read were ones it had already seen, against 7% for Astra. We estimate that these two "mechanical" inefficiencies account for roughly 25% of Carbon's excess runtime.
Conclusion
On difficult bug-fixing tasks, Carbon took close to an hour where Opus and Astra took minutes. We traced that gap to three sources:
- Slower inference. Each step takes longer, which explains 16–30% of the gap against Astra and about half against Opus.
- Unnecessary work. About half of Carbon's steps went on work the tickets never asked for: auditing code the fix didn't need and closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out.
- Mechanical inefficiencies. Fewer tool calls per step and frequent re-reading slow Carbon down; we estimate that fixing them alone would cut its runtime by roughly a quarter.

articles.title: I had AI read my entire field, Theoretical Astrophysics
articles.body:
I had AI read my entire field.
158,059 papers and 554,670 citations. Every paper with full text screened, 659 of the most important recomputed and checked, and every verified error followed through the papers that cite it. This is the map, and what it says about whether science corrects itself.
Errors that nobody fixed
I spent five years in this field doing my PhD at Caltech, and a few months of that went to errors in the literature that were already known. The equations my code was built on came from Bishop, Gómez, Lehner, Maharaj & Winicour, “High-powered gravitational news” (1997), the paper the subfield's characteristic codes descend from. People knew it had mistakes. The fixes were scattered through some 10,000 lines of intersecting email threads that contradicted each other, and the paper itself was never corrected. The best I could do was correct the record in my own papers: an appendix setting out the full set of equations, made consistent, and a parenthetical “with a sign error in s3 corrected” for anyone reading closely.
That is the limit of human literature review. Mine was not deep: my three thesis papers cite fewer than a hundred papers between them, in a field of tens of thousands. Nobody re-derives every equation they cite, referees check one paper once, and nobody is paid to go back and fix the original. So every student who builds on a broken paper pays the same tax, one at a time, and the correction lives in somebody's inbox. A machine can read the whole field, recompute it, and follow each error to every paper that copied it. So I had one do it. It found errors in my own papers too.
Every dot is a paper
Height is time: the 1960s at the bottom, this year at the top. Each faint line is a citation. The bright dots are the papers everything else leans on, ranked the way Google ranked the early web.
The seed is TAPIR, Caltech's theoretical astrophysics group, where I did my PhD: 4,093 papers by its 326 members since 2004. Add every paper they cite and every paper that cites them and you get 158,059 papers joined by 554,670 citations. The 49,301 drawn here are the ones tied to TAPIR at least three times over.
Watch it grow
The map holds 499 papers from the 1970s, 2,035 from the 1990s and 18,976 from the 2010s. The old layers are the survivors, the papers people working today still cite. Everything else from 1975 has already been forgotten, right or wrong.
Most of what this field knows was written in the last twenty years, by people who are still around to answer email. Hold that thought.
A subfield is a column
Nobody told the layout what numerical relativity is. Papers that cite each other pull together, so a subfield shows up as a column: the same few dozen people writing about the same problem year after year, each layer standing on the last.
There are 32 columns, from fast radio bursts to the Milky Way's halo.
Numerical relativity
Solving Einstein's equations on a computer until two black holes merge. 278 papers in this column, 71 of them TAPIR's, busiest in 2010.
Every subfield has a page: the questions it is organised around and whether each is open, contested or settled, who wrote the central papers and where, how fast it publishes, and which of its errors we traced.
Each open question also carries a flag for what today's AI could do about it. Of 155, a model judged 8 answerable now from data and codes that already exist, 119 ones AI would speed up, and 28 stuck waiting on a telescope or a detector.
Every paper gets screened
Reading a paper carefully costs a few dollars of model time. Screening one costs nothing, so every paper I could get the full text of got screened: 50,269 papers, 421 million words, checked for the fingerprints of the worst kinds of trouble. That covers 76% of the papers drawn here. Nothing before 1991 is on arXiv and journal-only papers aren't open, so the rest got only the checks that run on a database record. (Gold marks TAPIR's own papers.)
- Paper-mill language: none.
- Chatbot residue and hidden instructions to AI reviewers: none.
- Text shared between papers with no author in common: 43 pairs in 34,286 papers, led by successive survey catalogues and data releases. The rest are queued for a human look.
- Retractions: 13 among 184,733 papers with a DOI. None is TAPIR's.
- TODO and FIXME notes shipped to arXiv: 62 papers.
Astrophysics is relatively clean. Whatever is wrong with this literature, it isn't fraud. The one needle that moves is vocabulary: “delve”, “crucial” and friends are 2.5 times as common in 2025 as in 2016.
The 200 that matter get checked line by line
Citations are brutally unequal, and a few hundred papers carry the field. So the 200 most-cited TAPIR papers of 2006–2019 (gold) each got their own AI reviewer with the LaTeX source, tools to run its own calculations, and orders to recompute everything it could: re-derive the equations, test the limits, rebuild the numbers from the paper's own tables. It worked blind, with no access to errata or later papers.
A flag is not a finding. Only what a second reviewer upholds is called an error here.
Thirteen fixed, fifty-six through
About 136 of the 200 were revised between the first preprint and the published paper, so we read those first preprints the same way. 13 verified errors were in the preprint and gone from the journal version, fixed by the referee or by the authors on a second look (purple).
56 went through review and into the journal (gold). On this evidence peer review removes about one error in five. At least two of the thirteen were copied by later papers anyway, from the stale preprint.
A factor of four, 2005–2014
Smith, Kamionkowski & Cooray convert the gravitational waves left over from inflation into an energy density a detector could see. Two factors of one half went missing, so the answer is four times too big: a 6 in the denominator where the textbook has 24. This one was double-checked. The paper's numbers in the paper's formula reproduce its result; the same numbers in the standard formula give a quarter of it.
Watch the years run. Red papers copied the factor of four. The green one said it was wrong, in 2008. The copying carried on until 2014: six copies, one objection.
Five copies for every criticism
Then we cast the net wider. The same recompute-and-verify check, run on 459 more still-cited papers across the map, mostly highly cited ones that a cheaper first read had flagged, upheld 816 more errors. That makes 872 in 433 papers. 159 of them were copied, wrong value and all, into at least one later paper. Counting papers:
367 papers copied an error. 68 criticised one.
Only 47 of the 872 were ever criticised in print, and 21 of those kept being copied afterwards, by 51 more papers. These are floors: we read only the citing papers whose text we hold.
And 872 is a floor for the field too. Only 4% of the highly cited papers on the map got the thorough treatment so far. Scaled up from the papers that did, the likely number of undetected errors in this field's papers cited 100 or more times is about 34,000 (25,000–48,000). How that number is reached →
Half are still being copied 7 years later
How effective is peer review and publishing at detecting and expunging errors from the literature? We can actually measure it.
Share of copied errors still being copied, by years since the paper appeared. Band: 95% interval. 33 errors are old enough to be observed at year 10.
The curve is still at 52% at year 7 and crosses one half at year 8; at year 10 it is at 39%. Counting papers that lean on the affected result without showing which value they used, it crosses at year 9. The errors we traced most thoroughly last longer, crossing at year 10: a shallower search simply finds fewer late copies.
What finally stops an error? Of the 56 errors in the 200 papers read most closely, 52 are still in the latest arXiv version, where a fix is free. Of the 200 papers read most closely, the database records an erratum for 2. And of the 87 errors that did die out, 67 were never criticised by anyone. They faded when the subfield moved on, which retires right answers and wrong ones at the same rate.
4% of the papers that matter, so far
Every paper with open full text was screened and skimmed. The expensive check, the one that recomputes, has reached 659 papers, starting with the most cited. Each bar is the papers on the map with that many citations, filled by how far they have been read.
A field outgrows its errors. It rarely corrects them.
All of this would cost about $2,720 in model time bought at list price, roughly $3 per verified error. In practice it ran within a Claude Max subscription. The whole project, this field and the others, took about 4.9 billion tokens and about 44 hours of my time over 41 days. It is one field, read by a first-generation method, with limits spelled out on the method page. And it is not finished: the deep check has reached only 4% of the highly cited papers on the map, most cited first. The rest of the queue is a budget decision, and so is the next field.
Errors were found by one AI session and re-derived by a second, independent one, and each was confirmed in the version the journal published. Five were also double-checked step by step against the source. No person has checked any of them. As a test, 40 drawn at random went to a third session that saw only the paper and the passage: it found 33 of the 40 wrong, so some named here will not survive scrutiny. If we have your paper wrong, say so and we will fix it and say that we did.

articles.title: Engineering Vitals in the Age of AI
articles.body:
Every engineering organization is being asked the same question right now: is AI actually making us better at building software?
It’s a fair question. We’re spending real money on tokens and tooling, and we’re reshaping how our teams work. We should be able to say what we’re getting for it.
The answers I see tend to fall into two camps. The first counts activity: lines of code generated, tokens consumed, the percentage of code written by agents. The second skips straight to the destination, and declares that the only thing worth measuring is value.
LaunchDarkly’s recent Release Autopilot announcement is a good example of the second camp. It describes the goal they set for their AI software factory: maximize the valuable software reaching customers for each hour of human attention it takes to get it there.
That isn’t a goal. It’s an aspiration.
How do you count valuable software? Value shows up weeks or months after changes ship, and it’s the product of many decisions made across product, design, engineering, and sales. Value is a team sport. How do you count an hour of human attention? I won’t be the person who introduces timesheets for attention.
It’s worth looking at the evidence the same post offers. With roughly the same number of engineers, monthly merged pull requests more than doubled, and time spent in major and critical incidents fell by about 70%. Those are throughput and stability measures. They’re good evidence, and they sit a lot closer to a pull request count than they do to value.
This post is about what we’ve chosen to measure at Octopus, and why. None of it is revolutionary. But some of it is counter to the current product development zeitgeist.
Outcomes are made of outputs
Outcomes over outputs is one of the most repeated phrases in product development. It’s true that the outcome is ultimately the thing that matters. But the phrase obscures how we get to one.
Outcomes are realized through the continuous delivery of outputs. We make a decision, ship something, watch what happens, and decide again. It’s the OODA loop. The first thing we ship is almost never the most valuable thing. It helps us learn, pivot or persevere, and eventually reach a point where we’ve realized a lot of value.
You can’t ship just one thing and win. You also could ship infinite things and not win. You’ve got to produce outputs and go through the loop.
This is the value discovery loop. The faster we complete it, the more value we accumulate over time.
Velocity: the speed with which we complete the value discovery loop.
Outputs are a proxy to value.
Engineering vitals
Who is the primary driver of the value discovery loop? Engineering.
“But Besty, our product managers and designers are all shipping changes to our product these days thanks to Claude!” you might say. Congratulations to them - they are now also engineers, and their efforts will be reflected in engineering’s vitals.
One of the jobs of engineering leaders is to unblock and enable their organization’s teams to ship as effectively and efficiently as they can. Once you go past a handful of engineers, you can’t put your hand on your heart and say you are fulfilling this responsibility without having some sort of data to back it up.
At Octopus there have been multiple times when we have paused to measure something in our delivery pipeline, and discovered some healthy optimizations we could make.
Your vitals should give you insight into how effectively your engineering organization is producing outputs and maintaining its service level objectives. They will help you move beyond vibes, and to a more concrete view of how well you are delivering and contributing to your organization’s outcomes.
Why we rebooted our vitals
AI is a disruptive force, and at Octopus leaning into this disruption matters. AI is a lever - it can help us achieve more, and provide an increasingly better customer experience, without significantly increasing our costs. But even more importantly - our customers are undergoing the same disruption. Our customers are engineers - they ship software day in, day out, and most are somewhere along the same AI adoption journey we are on at Octopus. To truly empathize with our customers’ pain on this journey, we need to live it ourselves.
Our hypothesis about where software engineering is heading is simple: an overwhelming volume of change. We’re already seeing two-engineer teams become normal thanks to the leverage AI gives them, and the time it takes to build and ship is compressing.
We are rebooting our engineering vitals because our AI transformation is changing the shape of our work. I don’t use the word “transformation” hyperbolically here - the changes are actually transformational. We need to know whether the shifts we’re making in our AI-driven development lifecycle are helping us get through the value discovery loop faster, while maintaining our SLOs.
If the hypothesis holds, these are the questions we need to be able to answer:
- How frequently are we shipping changes and progressively releasing them to customers?
- Are our engineering feedback loops meeting our standards for speed and reliability?
- Is the volume of change increasing as we lean into agentic workflows, while headcount stays stable?
- Is work starting that previously wouldn’t have been done regularly, or at all?
- Is our operational burden shrinking? Fewer people, less time, less toil.
- Is quality improving at the same time?
- Are people still finding joy and satisfaction in their work, as the nature of that work changes?
These questions help us understand the effectiveness of our engineering organization, and help to identify which levers we might be able to pull if we spot things that are slowing us down.
AI adoption has its own set of measures that sit alongside our vitals - we will talk to these in a separate blog post.
The measures
We’ve divided our vitals into three areas.
Delivery objectives measure the effectiveness of our delivery pipeline and feedback loops. They’re measured per system, and the team that owns the system sets the service level objective (SLO).
Quality objectives measure the quality of what we ship, and the quality of our developer experience. They’re measured across the whole organization, and I as CTO own the SLOs.
Trends are measured across the whole organization, and deliberately have no SLO. We capture them because they give us insight, particularly when read alongside the objectives.
If you know the DORA metrics, most of this looks familiar. However there is one particular fight I’ll pick with DORA’s metrics - change failure rate does nothing to help you understand customer impact.
Do not obscure the customer impact of failure
We don’t measure change failure rate.
For a long time our change failure rate sat below 2%, which is healthy by any benchmark. Yet sometimes the failures that did occur still had significant customer impact. The signal said everything was fine. Our customers’ lived experience said otherwise.
AI makes this problem worse. A rate has a denominator, and the denominator is the thing we expect to explode. If we double the changes we merge and hold our failure rate steady, we’ve doubled the defects reaching customers, and the dashboard hasn’t moved.
Customers don’t experience a percentage. They experience the defect.
So we count. Every month we look at the number of Sev 0-2 defects that reached customers, and as leaders we dig into the specific issues behind the number. We can still derive a rate if we want one.
This only works if all work is tracked. If a defect has been merged to main and deployed, it’s logged with a severity, whether a customer found it or we did. We’re our own customer zero, so any issue that affects us affects a customer.
Trends without targets
We care about velocity, and need to reason about it in aggregate over time. In this, we take heed of Goodhart’s law for trends: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. So we don’t set goals for it.
Pull request volume is our proxy for velocity, and our window into the value discovery loop.
We care how quickly we are getting through the value discovery loop. We want to see a trend up and to the right as we lean further into agentic development.
We set other measurable goals that seek to impact velocity. An example might be the % of PRs that are shipped without human intervention.
Trends are particularly useful in combination with service level objectives. Pull request volume rising while Sev 0-2 counts hold flat and lead time stays steady tells a richer story than just understanding velocity is improving.
We’re in good company
While counter to some popular product development ideologies, none of this is particularly esoteric.
I’m a big fan and a regular reader of Gergely Orosz’s Pragmatic Engineer newsletter. In one publication, Laura Tacho and Gergely looked at how 18 tech companies measure the impact of AI, including Google, GitHub, Microsoft, Dropbox, and Monzo. Two findings stood out to me:
- Most of the types of measures look the same as they did before AI. The companies getting clear answers are the ones that had already invested in understanding their engineering performance.
- Almost every company pairs a measure of speed with a measure of quality, so each keeps the other in check.
More recent data tells the same story with bigger numbers. Atlassian’s write-up of DX data from more than 500 companies reports that median pull request throughput has doubled. It also reports that pull request size grew 122% in four quarters, engineers’ confidence in their changes dropped, and the share of capacity going to new customer value moved by a single percentage point.
That’s the overwhelming volume of change arriving, without the value arriving with it. It’s also why pull request volume is a trend for us and not a goal.
The same write-up describes Dropbox pointing its unlocked capacity at long-deferred maintenance, like language migrations and dependency upgrades. That’s one of our own questions being answered: work is starting that previously wouldn’t have been done.
There’s one place we’re out of step. Nearly all of these companies track change failure rate as their quality measure, and we’ve chosen counts. I’ve explained why above.
And to be fair to LaunchDarkly, their numbers fit this pattern too. Merged pull requests up, incident time down, headcount flat. Speed and quality, measured side by side. It’s good evidence that their machine is working. Whether the software was valuable is a different question, answered somewhere else.
Speaking of LaunchDarkly, did you know Octopus now has Feature Flags? Octopus feature flags are available in all license tiers at no additional cost, are built on OpenFeature, and are a natural fit for organizations deploying with a high frequency, who want more control over the release of changes to their customers and users.
Conclusion
AI hasn’t changed what makes an engineering organization effective. It has changed how much flows through one, and how quickly a weakness gets exposed.
Measuring value per hour of human attention is a fine thing to want. But value is a lagging signal with many owners, and you can’t steer your organization by it week to week.
So start with the measuring what you can steer. Know how long it takes to get a change into customers’ hands, how quickly you recover when a change is wrong, how many serious defects reached customers this month, and whether the volume of change is growing while those numbers hold.
When you can answer those questions on demand, you can then raise your gaze: if your measures are healthy and the needle still isn’t moving, you know where to look next.
Measure the efficiency of your engineering machine. Then set your sights on value.

articles.title: Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
articles.body:
Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year. The announcement was made by interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress during an earnings call on Tuesday, marking a notable shift for the company that, under former CEO Jensen Huang, fought for the right to ship its powerful Hopper architecture H200 chips to China.
Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
After former CEO Jensen Huang fought for US approval to sell H200 chips in China, Nvidia is now walking away.
“Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data center products to China,” Kress said. She did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing its H200 processor shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future.
The pivot comes after Huang stepped down from his position as Nvidia CEO last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, one with a woman who was suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia already faced difficulties around offloading the AI chips prior to this scandal, however. Concerns were raised about failings to properly vet Chinese companies that were approved to handle the H200 AI chips. Reuters also reported earlier this month that around 600,000 H200 chips were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports, with China seeking to reduce its dependency on US technology.

articles.title: US Officially a Measles Endemic Country
articles.body:
US Officially a Measles Endemic Country 113
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years.
Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has previously said losing elimination status won't lead to changes in the federal response.
"We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities," Schwartz said on Tuesday. "Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks."

articles.title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
articles.body:
Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- American Heart Association
- Summary:
- A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation.
- Share:
Energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.
The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.
Researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.
Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health
The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.
Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.
A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).
However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.
Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.
"These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products."
FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events
To investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.
The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.
Several differences stood out in the analysis:
- Cardiac arrest: Reports involving caffeine and stimulant products were approximately 11 times more likely to mention cardiac arrest than reports involving products without these ingredients.
- Heart attacks: Heart attacks appeared about 4.5 times more frequently in reports associated with energy drinks and stimulant supplements.
- Abnormal heart rhythms: Reports involving stimulant products were roughly four times more likely to include ventricular arrhythmias (abnormal rhythm in the heart's lower pumping chambers) or heart palpitations.
- Other cardiovascular symptoms: The researchers also identified higher reporting frequencies for rapid heart rate (nearly 3 times more often), chest pain (2.71 times more often) and fainting (about 2 times more often).
- Young adults: Approximately 45% of cardiovascular event reports involving caffeine and stimulant products concerned adults between ages 18 and 34.
- Men and women: Comparable patterns appeared in reports submitted for both sexes.
These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.
"Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula said.
Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable
One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.
Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.
How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.
These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.
Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?
Although the results raise important questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.
"This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," said Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events."
Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.
Because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.
How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports
The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.
Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.
Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).
Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.
The researchers also highlighted important limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.
Just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.
Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.
Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.
Story Source:
Materials provided by American Heart Association. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Evidence Studio is a complete enterprise business intelligence platform built around Evidence Core, combining an AI analytics agent with access control, enterprise security, and governance. Evidence Studio powers analytics at hundreds of organizations.
Evidence was founded in 2021 by Sean Hughes and Adam McAskill. Prior to founding Evidence, Sean and Adam built the data science team at Canada's leading private equity fund.
