articles.title: Satya Nadella Says He's AGI-Pilled Now
articles.body:
Satya Nadella Says He's AGI-Pilled Now (theverge.com) 8
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Verge: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he's AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. "I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy's organization around AGI?" he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco. But Nadella doesn't think frontier models like Claude are conscious. "I don't think so," he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman's view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic's team has "wireheaded" themselves, and that this approach is dangerous. Nadella wasn't quite as firm about it. "It's a good debate," he said. "I'm not sort of dogmatic about it. What I'm saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?"
I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter's questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status. "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us." "Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be," he said. "But remember, the model has no limits. It'll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it."
Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. "If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?" he asked. "If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That's the debate." "I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one -- at least in a democracy -- can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there's only capital and there's no labor. I mean, I don't know, that's not an economy." "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic."

articles.title: Nvidia says its open source AI strategy remains intact after Jensen Huang’s exit
articles.body:
Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress reaffirmed the company’s commitment to open source AI during Tuesday’s earnings call with analysts — the first since CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation.
“At Nvidia, we are committed to fostering a vibrant open model ecosystem, so every country, company, and industry can build its own intelligence,” Kress said in her opening remarks. She also noted that open models were accelerating AI adoption, citing a 35-fold year-over-year surge in weekly token volume on OpenRouter, including a 3.5-fold increase over the past three months.
Kress also spoke about Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face, a platform for open source AI models that the company agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September, in what would be the second-largest acquisition in Nvidia’s history.
The platform, which serves more than 18 million developers and 200,000 companies, is still on track to join Nvidia, despite Huang’s ouster. Huang had heavily advocated for open source AI technology. His departure had raised questions about the company’s future approach to open source AI models, with Hugging Face’s CEO calling Huang’s departure “a sad day,” and promising to “keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever.”
So far, Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face appear unchanged. The acquisition was not directly addressed during the Q&A portion of the earnings call.
“Together, we will scale its platform and make intelligence more open, more capable, and more accessible,” said Kress of Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face.
Last week, Nvidia founder Huang resigned from his position as CEO following news about his extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. He’s also accused of having extramarital affairs with two direct reports and is now set to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving. Meanwhile, the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, The WSJ reported.
Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads. On today’s call, Kress noted that Nemotron is now the “most widely used U.S. open model on OpenRouter,” and it’s “where developers start to build their own intelligence.”
“That foundation is empowering the ecosystem,” she said.
Correction: Due to a typo, an earlier version of this article incorrectly stated the number of developers served by Hugging Face; it is 18 million, not 118 million.

articles.title: How The Verge is picking which Black Friday deals to share
articles.body:
For the past month, we’ve been inundated with Black Friday deals, signaling what’s to come on the biggest shopping day of the year in the US. We routinely get dozens of press releases a day, coming from brands big and small that hope that we’ll publicize these offers. Of course, the companies would prefer that we don’t do any research on these deals to see if they’re actually good, and most don’t provide any of the necessary context we’re looking for when vetting them.
How The Verge is picking which Black Friday deals to share
Ahead of the busiest shopping day of the year, here’s how we determine which discounts are worth your attention.
Most indicators of a good deal are confusing — not just for us, but for anyone who’s shopping. Groundwork Collaborative recently published its findings about the unclear manner in which Amazon displays deals. Its researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, and they claim that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon didn’t offer savings during the actual shopping events. The investigation also found that nearly a tenth of the deals it examined were more expensive during the sales events than on some days in the month leading up to them.
Something we commonly see on Amazon and attempt to correct for in our coverage are good deals with inflated discount claims. As in, the original retail amount (the “list” price) is sometimes higher than the usual day-to-day price to make the savings seem more substantial. Sometimes, the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) is what’s shown, though that’s not always the case.
In a recent statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow, an unattributed Amazon spokesperson shared that its “List Price” can also be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork Collaborative’s research states, and is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers. However, in our experience, the confusing way pricing and discounts are communicated isn’t limited to Amazon.
The group’s findings show how easy it is to distrust the prices you see, especially online, where dynamic pricing sometimes comes into play. Regardless of retailer practices, we understand the importance of curating what you see on The Verge with care.
Vetting deals for coverage consideration is a big, albeit invisible, part of our jobs, even outside of big shopping events. Most of what we’re pitched day to day, or what we see in our respective feeds, never hits the site because it doesn’t meet our standards. Even when the deal is for a product we’ve tested and really enjoy — our north star for what to cover on the deals front — that alone doesn’t guarantee coverage. We often skip covering deals that aren’t as good as a retailer or brand made them seem. Or maybe the deal is good, but it returns every week, lasts only a few hours, or it’s available only with a premium membership. Alternatively, the deal might only be available from a retailer none of us has heard of or shopped at. Needless to say, we consider a ton of factors.
With Black Friday coming up, you deserve transparency from us so you know — whether it’s this month or a random day in February — that you’re looking at an actual deal when you visit our site. The most basic criteria we use to judge whether a deal is good is whether we like the product enough to write about it and whether its price has dropped. Then we assess whether the discount is actually worth your attention. That part of the conversation has become a little complicated in the past year. RAMageddon and the ripple effects of higher tariffs have, in some cases, substantially impacted pricing and, by extension, the deals we cover.
We follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass
For products hit by recent price hikes, the new deal prices sometimes amount to the original sticker price, or close to it. Several of us would nod our heads with you if you think, “Hey, that’s not a deal; that’s just the original price. I’m no fool!” But it’s also technically a deal for many of us who are just trying to save wherever possible. Along those lines, we’ll sometimes highlight ways to save on digital or physical goods by buying discounted gift cards, which can be used to buy in-demand products. These methods are the only way to get any kind of deal on Grand Theft Auto VI before launch, for example.
To help us stay aware of price drops, we also use free tracking tools like CamelCamelCamel and Keepa, which provide an independent read on Amazon’s historical pricing. (You can use them, too!) They’ll alert us when a product we like — and that we know you’ll probably like — goes on sale. Amazon also has its own Alexa for Shopping tool, which can show up to a year of pricing data and perform several other AI chatbot-like actions, including automatically buying products on your behalf. In my experience, Amazon’s historical pricing data usually aligns with non-Amazon-affiliated companies. However, none of them are perfect. Even the third-party tools we use don’t always display the record-low prices we’ve covered, for whatever reason. All of this to say, there are a lot of ins and outs, but we follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass.
We cast a fairly large net for products across a range of categories ahead of the holidays, including some that don’t often get much play on The Verge. However, of the thousands of deals that we’ve seen ahead of Black Friday, you’re seeing the mere dozens of standouts that we’ve tested or used in our personal lives within each category — headphones, TVs, gaming accessories, smart home tech, etc. — that meet our criteria for being good products at noteworthy prices.

articles.title: This Is the Perfect Gift for Every Kind of Cook (at Every Price Point!)
articles.body:
This Is the Perfect Gift for Every Kind of Cook (at Every Price Point!)
Some gifts are unwrapped, enjoyed for a season, and tucked away. Others immediately become woven into how life is lived for decades: the Dutch oven pulled out for slow-simmered Sunday suppers, the fluted pie dish brought to the table for milestone birthdays, or the stovetop kettle whistling in sync with quiet morning rituals.
Made for making since 1925, Le Creuset has spent a century creating cookware for those who find genuine joy in the kitchen. Every enameled cast-iron vessel, sturdy stoneware dish, and refined accessory is crafted with intention: made to last, built to be shared, and designed to anchor the moments that stay with us long after we clear the table. Whether you’re shopping for a dedicated home baker, an outdoor grill enthusiast, or a passionate host who turns dinner into an event, Le Creuset pieces are thoughtfully made to give and cherish for a lifetime.
To help you make a lasting impression this season, here’s the ultimate Le Creuset gift guide for every price point to inspire new kitchen traditions for generations to come.
For the Chef
Serious home cooks rely on resilient, high-performance cookware that can pivot effortlessly from blazing stove burners to low-and-slow oven braises. These durable staples will quickly become the pieces they reach for every day.
Under $50: Every great home chef knows that a calm, inspired cooking flow starts with smart mise en place. Sized perfectly for measuring spices, herbs, and minced garlic, the Vancouver Pinch Bowls Set helps every recipe shine. Glazed with Le Creuset’s scratch- and stain-resistant enamel, they’re thoughtful and functional for any culinary enthusiast.
Under $150: Crafted with a responsive aluminum core sandwiched between layers of gleaming stainless steel, the Signature Stainless Steel Fry Pan delivers flash-searing heat with surgical precision. It’s an essential tool for reducing pan sauces, browning proteins, and perfecting delicate omelets without sticking.
Under $350: With shallow sides and a broad base, the 3.5 qt Signature Round Wide Oven is a workhorse for searing large batches of meat in a single layer before gently braising them to fork-tenderness. It’s an essential kitchen centerpiece that makes every meal memorable.
For the Baker
Baking is an act of love grounded in patience, precision, and dependable techniques. These heirloom-worthy stoneware and cast-iron essentials are made to make every recipe shine, helping your favorite baker create patisserie-level showstoppers.
Under $50: A charming festive detail with a real culinary purpose. Crafted from dense stoneware, the Christmas Tree Pie Vent releases steam from bubbling fruit pies during baking, eliminating soggy bottom crusts and boil-overs. It’s a joyful, practical stocking stuffer that spreads cheer with every bake.
Under $150: Inspired by a century of artisanal craftsmanship, the versatile Heritage 3-Piece Rectangular Baking Dish Set nesting trio is the ultimate foundation for sweet and savory holiday staples. Crafted from durable stoneware that distributes heat evenly without burning delicate edges, it effortlessly transitions from baking bubbly cinnamon rolls, berry crisps, and gratins in the oven straight to a festive table spread.
Under $350: The Signature Oval Bread Oven is the ultimate showstopper for the artisan breadmaker. Designed specifically for bâtards, sandwich breads, and longer sourdough or artisan loaves, its domed enameled cast-iron lid traps steam to yield maximum rise, an open crumb, and a crisp, crackling crust every time.
For the Grill Master
Cooking over an open flame calls for cookware with rugged construction that thrives under intense heat. Give the outdoor enthusiast gear engineered to handle fire grates, charcoal grills, and smokers with uncompromising culinary control. (Even if they’re just making dinner on the patio.)
Under $50: Built specifically to withstand the searing temperatures of live-fire cooking, the heavy-duty Outdoor Slotted Turner is made to last through season after season at the grates. It’s a professional-grade outdoor staple that will make a lasting impression on any backyard barbecuer. (It also has a built-in bottle opener on the handle, which we think is extraordinarily clever.)
Under $150: A solid Butcher Block is one of those clever gifts they didn’t know they needed. Upgrade their plastic cutting board with a thick, knife-friendly hardwood surface that can handle slicing whole smoked briskets, carving turkeys, or breaking down roasted cuts.
Under $350: If we could gift one thing to a grill master, it would be the Alpine Outdoor Collection Rectangular Griddle designed specifically for the intense demands of outdoor gas grills, charcoal embers, and campfire cooking. Its durable matte black enamel coating requires no seasoning, making it easy to sear delicate fish, fire-charred vegetables, and sizzling morning bacon in the open air.
For the Host
For those who love to bring people together, cooking is all about connection, atmosphere, and the joy of welcoming friends around the table. These versatile, presentation-forward pieces bridge the gap between oven and dining room, making hospitality feel effortless. They may even put your gift to immediate use!
Under $50: Topped with an elegant gold star knob, the Noël Collection Mini Cocotte brings instant magic to group gatherings. Use it for baking individual French onion soups, serving baked dips, or delighting guests with personal lava cakes at their place settings.
Under $150: Substantial and generously scaled, this glazed stoneware Serving Platter features elevated rim detailing to keep savory pan juices and dressings contained. It turns holiday roasts, grilled skewers, and colorful antipasti boards into an undeniable visual feast.
Under $350: The centerpiece for lively winter gatherings, the enameled cast-iron Alpine Signature Fondue Set is made to make new traditions. It maintains gentle, even warmth for molten Gruyère or rich chocolate fondues, inviting family and friends to linger, dip, and connect long after dinner is served.
Bonus Favorites
If you want to present an iconic, enduring masterpiece that becomes part of a home’s story forever, look no further than Le Creuset’s legendary enameled cast iron Dutch ovens. The elongated design of the Traditional Oval Dutch Oven easily accommodates whole chickens, pork loins, and long roasts with room to spare.
For a festive heritage piece you’ll look forward to using every year, the Noël Collection Holiday Tree Signature Round Dutch Oven is an intricate seasonal heirloom embossed with evergreen motifs and crowned with a gleaming gold star knob. And last but certainly not least, the 5.5 qt Signature Round Dutch Oven is the undisputed icon of the culinary world. It’s sized to feed families, celebrate holidays, and simmer memories for a lifetime of shared meals.

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now 1 light-day away
articles.body:
After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: The spacecraft is now officially 1 light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, “very, very far.” The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet — equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours.
NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now 1 light-day away
It’s taken Voyager 1 almost 50 years to journey farther from Earth than light can travel in 24 hours.
It’s the farthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1’s journey isn’t over yet. It’s been heading toward a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. That star is 17 light-years away, meaning Voyager 1 won’t pass by it for around 40,000 years, despite traveling at nearly 38,000 mph.
The light-day milestone is a remarkable feat alone, but especially so when you consider that Voyager 1 is still operational. NASA has done well to keep it functioning, and it can continue to send back readings on plasma waves, magnetic fields, and space-bound particles, though it now takes radio signals an entire day to travel between Earth and the spacecraft. Voyager 2, which launched 16 days before its twin, is also expected to reach a distance of 1 light-day away from Earth, but not until 2035.

articles.title: Well, Here It Is, My First GoFundMe!
articles.body:
Well, Here It Is, My First GoFundMe!
Posted on November 18, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 18 Comments
Though I had thought that starting a GoFundMe was certainly a possibility I’d have to consider further down the line, that time has come much sooner than I anticipated. Who knew caring for cats was so expensive? (Spoiler alert: all of us.)
I honestly struggled with the idea of it. Who am I to take on a task no one asked me to, and then ask strangers for money? It just didn’t seem right for me to ask for funds when times are so tough. Why donate towards random stray cats when gas is so expensive?
But then, as I continued to share with y’all, you all made me realize that people do want to help. That’s why GoFundMe exists, because oftentimes people genuinely want to assist in others’ journeys. I personally have donated to nineteen GoFundMes in the past, but now I must admit that I am the one in need of help.
Everything you’ve been seeing me post, I have paying for out of pocket. One commenter mentioned me spending all of my father’s money, but I just want to make it clear that everything I’ve done has been out of my own checking account, which these days is genuinely not looking too hot.
It’s hard to ask for funds when you all see me going to nice dinners and trying out new products, but this sudden upfront cost of thousands in vet bills is more than I ever accounted for.
So, at y’all’s behest and my humble request, here is my GoFundMe for the colony cats.
Thank you all for joining me in this journey. It is something I dove head first into, and while I don’t regret it, I could’ve benefitted from more careful planning.
Please know that I appreciate all of your encouragement and support, whether it’s financial or kind comments. Let’s get these cats their forever homes.
-AMS

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI does something impossible — it lives up to the hype
articles.body:
How do you follow a game like Grand Theft Auto V? Thirteen years ago, Rockstar’s crime-fueled epic went on to redefine what an open-world game could be and became an enormous success, selling more than 230 million copies across three generations of game consoles. It sits just behind Tetris and Minecraft on the list of the best-selling games of all time, and its lucrative online mode has helped it remain popular for well over a decade.
Grand Theft Auto VI does something impossible — it lives up to the hype
Thirteen years later, Rockstar has crafted a worthy successor to GTA V and the new standard-bearer for open-world games.
That level of success has allowed Rockstar to take its time with a sequel, which has further increased the hype around the next GTA. A series of major leaks and delays only exacerbated this. At a time when much of the video game industry is struggling, the next edition of GTA stands alone, a cultural moment so big (almost) everybody has been forced to get out of the way. The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen.
Even more remarkable? The game was actually worth the wait.
At this point I’ve spent nearly 80 hours in Leonida, GTA VI’s fictional take on Florida. And what I’ve experienced is a game that combines the wide-open freedom offered in GTA V with the remarkable level of immersion from the studio’s 2018 release Red Dead Redemption 2, while also improving on both qualities. At the same time, it’s also the most mature GTA game Rockstar has ever made, merging the criminal antics and absurdist humor the series is known for with a love story that gives you new ways to interact with the world and new reasons for wanting to push forward. This is the GTA game the studio has been building toward for its entire existence.
Let’s start with that new premise. GTA V introduced the idea of multiple protagonists to the series, and VI takes that concept in a different direction. It’s a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired story about Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, two small-time criminals who meet while, of course, stealing a car. It’s the most GTA-possible meet-cute. The idea is that you can play as both characters individually and also build their relationship over the course of the game. Things start out relatively slow. At the outset, Lucia is in prison, and you play solely as Jason, getting things ready for when she gets out. You can fix up your ramshackle house — that involves actually nailing down new stairs and rolling out paint on the walls — and also start building up a nest egg through means that are not exactly legal.
Jason and Lucia’s relationship grows naturally over the course of the game, but it’s also a slow buildup to becoming the inseparable pair they were by the end of my playthrough. GTA VI approaches most of the experience with confident and deliberate pacing. Even when you control them individually, the characters are often together, either just hanging out or partnering for a crime. And being able to play as both is one of the game’s standout features. But I didn’t get to that point in the game until almost 17 hours in. Before that, you play as both leads mostly solo, learning who they are as people, before you’re given free rein to switch between the two.
What’s great about the premise is how seamlessly it fits with what you’re actually doing in the game. There’s some bigger-picture stuff that I won’t spoil, but generally speaking, the main goal in GTA VI is to make a lot of money so that Jason and Lucia can get out of the criminal life for good and retire somewhere comfortably. And outside of the big story missions, you’re largely free to choose how you go about that. You can rob jewelry stores, steal cars, raid drug dens, or even search for hidden treasure at the bottom of the sea. Over the course of the game you’ll also meet different criminals who serve as fences, so you can sell them whatever you’ve got to build up your savings account. Sometimes they’ll even text you targets that are particularly lucrative.
The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play. I’m not a big fan of armed robbery, for instance. There are just so many things that can go wrong, and I almost always end up killing some innocent bystander when I try to escape. But I love getaway chases, and so stealing cars became my main form of income. Most importantly, though, this structure gives you a lot of reasons to go out in the world and explore. The missions take you all over the map — which is actually entirely accessible from the very beginning, if you choose to play that way — including not only the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City, but also tourist beaches, swamps, trailer parks, and a wild variety of other locations, each with its own landscape to explore and characters to meet.
To be clear: Despite being larger, more mature, and more lifelike, this is still very much GTA. This is a game about chaos and crime. This comes across in a few ways. First, there are those smaller missions where you never really know how things will play out. The cashier at the pawn shop you’re robbing might have a shotgun, or you might accidentally smash into a big rig during a high-speed getaway. The world itself is full of unpredictable moments that force you to think on your feet. Several times I stopped my car to talk to an NPC whose vehicle broke down on the side of the road. In one instance the driver just swore at me to leave her alone. In another, I got pulled into an entire storyline involving a delivery driver who needed help to keep her AI chatbot manager off her back. I delivered her packages and ended up dealing with everything from porch pirates to tigers.
The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play.
There are also the multistep heists, which return from GTA V more intricate and complex. These are the big scores and involve several different missions: You spend time getting the right gear and gathering all of the information you need to actually pull them off. Even some of the sub-missions can be gigantic, including one where you have to go undercover for weeks of in-game time to get everything you need in order. But the payoff is incredible. The heists play out like over-the-top action set-pieces, as if they were pulled out of a Christopher Nolan movie like Tenet or Inception (but without all of the sci-fi twists). Even better, all of the missions in the game feel streamlined with a new checkpoint system that allows you to spend less time replaying sequences after failing, and if you fail too many times, you can just skip that mission altogether. There are still a few too many prolonged shootouts, but the checkpoints mean they’re much less tedious than in past GTA games.
All of this action is crammed into a world that isn’t just huge, but also feels more alive than ever before. Like in Red Dead Redemption 2, you can talk with any NPC, but here you have more options, letting you either greet them or, if you feel like causing trouble, taunt them. Most of the time you’ll get a simple “hey” or someone begging for a few dollars. Other times you’ll get pulled into a fistfight or an unexpected storyline. Once, on my way to buy new clothes, I accidentally bumped into some gang members who followed me inside the store, and I had no choice but to fight them. The owner of the shop called the cops, and so I figured if I was in this much trouble, I might as well empty the register. What started out as a quest to find a cool T-shirt turned into a high-speed escape from the cops.
Another important thing to note: While the game retains the series’ satirical tone in many ways, the humor doesn’t punch down like in past GTAs, at least from what I’ve played. Instead it makes fun of stuff that deserves to be made fun of: men’s rights activists, NFT bros, conspiracy theorists, Bryan Johnson.
But what really makes the world so special are all the small, meaningful details. Changing your clothes is a lot of fun, but it also helps keep the cops off your back when you’re wanted. Eating and drinking helps improve your physical abilities. And, this being GTA, you can use just about every kind of vehicle imaginable. That includes taking the bus, which runs on a predetermined route, making stops along the way. You can rent electric scooters, and just like in real life, they’re a menace clogging up the streets of Vice City. Your cars even need to be gassed up from time to time.
It’s a careful balancing act. These details make the world feel more nuanced and textured, but they’re also minor enough that they don’t feel tedious. This isn’t The Sims where you’re constantly monitoring your characters’ bodily functions. Usually, I only remembered to eat when the fitness app on my phone told me I needed more protein, and I didn’t once have a car break down because I forgot to fill up the tank. These smaller mechanisms are just enough to add a sense of realism without getting in the way of the action. You can also ignore a lot of them; at no point do you need to shower, but you might hear some snide remarks from your partner if you don’t.
Perhaps the best example of this is the in-game smartphone, which is integrated into the lives of both characters in a thoughtful, plausible way. Crime bosses might text you a location to meet up, for instance, and you can add it to your GPS and head over. Or Lucia might text Jason a link to a funny video, which you can then open in a social networking app, and you can even read the comments. Smartphones have become a common user interface in games, but in GTA VI it’s a part of the world; the game doesn’t pause when you pull out your phone, meaning that if you get a text while you’re driving, you can either pull over and read it or try to text and drive.
Despite spending more than 70 hours in the world, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience
I also found these details, like the phone calls and texts between the couple, pulled me further into the story of Jason and Lucia and made me feel closer to both of them. When the two are together, you can press one of the shoulder buttons to make them hold hands. As long as you keep pressing it, they stay together. At first I used this strategically, imagining that if a couple holding hands was casing a jewelry store, it would be much less conspicuous. But eventually, as I grew to know the couple, it just became a thing I did without thinking about it. These two are crazy in love; of course they’re going to hold hands all the time. You can even do little things like make a coffee and choose to hand it to your partner instead of drinking it yourself, and all of these acts improve your relationship, which in turn impacts how the characters relate to each other and how some of the narrative elements play out.
You don’t have to do any of that. There are just so many ways to interact with the world that different players will find their own things to fixate on. For me, it was a lot of holding hands and drinking coffee every morning. Someone else might get really into fashion or hunting or customizing cars. I barely touched on any of those elements and still felt like I had a substantial experience.
Jason and Lucia are two very different people, each with their own kinds of stories to explore within the game. The big missions are cinematic heists that usually involve some combination of the two. But there are large, branching narratives that are only playable as one or the other character. Jason, for instance, has an old friend who is trying to start a record label in the back room of a strip club. As with the best GTA stories, the tale steadily escalates until you’re feuding with a famous rapper and facing down a number of life-or-death situations. Lucia, meanwhile, has to deal with her mom’s quest to become a real estate agent that gets her caught up with a violent gang, and her best friend pulling her into a pyramid scheme that seems very much like a cult but turns out to be something even more ridiculous. These storylines are so big and absorbing that I would often forget about the main campaign for long periods of time.
It’s not that there are zero issues with the game. The combat is still clunky, and the weapon wheel is still frustrating; there were multiple times when I accidentally equipped a flashlight instead of a shotgun when in the heat of battle. I also ran into a handful of small bugs, like dead bodies comically flopping around or a coffee mug that was stuck floating in a hotel room. But given how ambitious GTA VI is, and how badly things can go with large open games, the relative lack of technical issues during my playthrough is impressive. Even better: I played the game on a launch-version PS5, and it ran just fine.
Back in 2018, I called Red Dead Redemption 2 “the most convincing open-world game ever made,” and over the last eight years that has remained true. There have been great examples of the form since then — Elden Ring, Tears of the Kingdom, Control Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077 (eventually) — but none that approach the scale and detail of Rockstar’s works. Certainly none that attempted to do it in anything like the contemporary, real-world setting that has made GTA so pervasive. Now that mantle has been passed to GTA VI.
To give you a sense of how big this game is, despite spending more than 70 hours in the world and completing the main story, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience. And I just spent 2,500 words explaining how good GTA VI is without even touching on some of the best parts: the incredible selection of music, the hilarious talk radio stations, the pitch-perfect casting, the lifelike graphics. There are full-on TV shows, books, and video games that you can experience inside of the game. The most pretentious indie game of 2026? It exists in GTA VI.
For the last decade the idea of GTA VI has been inseparable from the hype around it. All of the noise caused by leaks, delays, and the protracted development time has turned the game into something larger than life, an experience hailed as the biggest game of all time before it even launched. It really seemed like no project could live up to the level of scrutiny that GTA VI has been and will be subjected to. But now we can forget all of that, because GTA VI is actually here. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it.
Grand Theft Auto VI launches on the PS5 and Xbox on November 19th.

articles.title: Talos Linux
articles.body:
Talos Linux is free and open source under MPL-2.0. Talos Enterprise Linux is the same OS. What the enterprise tier adds is proof, indemnity, and someone to call: the assurance, compliance evidence, and support that security and procurement teams need to sign off.
Open stays open. Enterprise adds assurance and service on top of the same open-source OS. Same code, same MPL-2.0, your hardware. Security is never gated behind the paid tier.
Trusted by enterprise platform teams
In production across regulated, sovereign, and mission-critical environments.
Infrastructure that can’t drift, and can’t be logged into.
Most fleets are held together by hand, and the gaps are where they break. Talos removes the gaps by design, the same across every cluster and every site.
Minimal
Minimal by design
Fewer than 50 binaries, just enough to run Kubernetes. Minimal attack surface, minimal CVEs.
API-only
No SSH, no shell
Every node interaction goes through a secured gRPC API with mutual TLS. Nothing to log into.
Immutable
Read-only & ephemeral
Nothing is written to disk at runtime, nothing persists between reboots. A reboot returns the node to its declared state.
Declarative
One YAML, whole machine
The entire machine state is defined declaratively. No configuration-management tools to maintain.
Atomic
Unified lifecycle
OS and Kubernetes upgrade together as one atomic, rollback-safe image. The same swap from day zero on.
Hardened
Secure by default
mTLS on all API access, CIS guidelines applied out of the box, SELinux and trusted boot included.
Talos Enterprise Linux: clear the security review. Keep the open-source OS.
Everything Talos Linux does, plus Omni fleet management, the audit evidence, indemnity, and response times that get an open-source OS through enterprise procurement. Built for NIS2 and CRA.
Compliance
FIPS & regulatory fit
FIPS 140-3 compliant builds and a posture built for the frameworks auditors ask about.
FIPS 140-3 compliant builds
NIS2 & CRA-aligned posture
CIS benchmark alignment
Supply chain
Artifacts security teams demand
Evidence tied to the exact image you run, traceable back to source.
Schematic-specific SBOM per release
Curated VEX, not auto-generated noise
Signed build attestation
OCI-compatible distribution
Support
24/7/365, with targets
The people who wrote the code, not a tier-1 helpdesk.
CVE SLAs with response targets by severity
Direct access to Sidero engineering
Dedicated Slack channel
Upgrade & migration assistance
Legal
Commercial IP indemnity

articles.title: Human.md
articles.body:
BRIANA (MAZZIO) MAY · APR 28, 2026
HUMAN.md
          > a working manifesto. notes-to-self, mostly.
> not a thinkpiece. not a thread. not a deck.
> last edited at the kitchen table, coffee #2.
## what this file is
A reminder, in plain text, of what I think humans actually bring to the table now that the machines are very good and getting better every day.
I keep coming back to the word "taste" and I keep finding it too small. Taste is the surface. There is a whole engine underneath it, and that engine is the part the model can't have. Yet. Maybe ever. I don't know. I'm not in that argument. I'm in this one:
## the actual job
### 1. break the rule on purpose
Models are trained on the average. The average is the floor, not the ceiling. Our job is not to conform a little better than the last person who conformed. Our job is to know the rule cold, and then break it on purpose, in public, with a reason.
Symmetry is a rule. Break it.
Three-act structure is a rule. Break it.
"Don't shoot into the sun" is a rule. Break it.
If you can't say why you broke it, you didn't break it, you just missed.
### 2. find the thing in the weird place
Inspiration does not live in the first ten image-search results. It lives in:
- a misprinted parking ticket
- the way your grandfather folded a napkin
- an obscure Victorian zoetrope of a cat
- the back of a menu in a town you can't pronounce
- the tension in Rene Magritte's "The Son of Man", 1946
A model averages the internet. A human walks somewhere strange and brings back something unexpected.
### 3. advocate for the human and humanity
Every brief now has an invisible third party at the table. Someone has to keep saying "and what does this feel like for the person on the other end of it." Someone has to keep saying "how is humanity better through the birthing of this idea?" That's the job. Not "is it on-brand." Not "does it convert." What does it feel like? what good does it do?
If you aren't there saying it, no one will. The model certainly won't.
### 4. design for emotional resonance, not correctness
Tension. Surprise. Restraint. The pause before the punchline. The photograph that's almost in focus. The sentence that ends one beat earlier than you expected.
These are not bugs. These are the entire reason anyone remembers anything. "Correct" is the lowest bar in the building. Step over it and keep walking.
### 5. seek delight, not delivery
I would rather make one thing that makes someone laugh out loud on a train than ten things that "meet the brief." At the very least, it needs to make ME laugh. This is a personal bias.
If it's not at least a little bit fun, why are we here?
### 6. experiment ruthlessly, ship more than you opine
A working sketch beats a confident take. Every time.
A bad first draft beats a brilliant unwritten one. Every time.
A weird little prototype beats a slide deck about prototyping.
Every. Time.
Make 50 things. Throw away 47. Talk about the 3.
Do not, under any circumstances, become a person who mostly posts opinions about other people's work.
### 7. own the output. fully.
If the AI output is bad, the AI did not fail you. You failed it. You picked the tool. You wrote the prompt. You accepted the result. You shipped it.
The fix is not a better model, or a return to tools of the past. The fix is a sharper you. Sharpen yourself. Sharpen your ideas. Sharpen the way you say what you mean, because the gap between what you wanted and what came back is almost always a gap in you, not in the tool.
Powerful tools reward the people who showed up sharp, iterate, spend extra time on the vision. They expose the people who didn't. AI is not the great equalizer, it is the great amplifier.
### 8. design with it, not next to it
Watching the generation happen is not the work.
Prompting once and accepting the result is not the work.
The work is the back-and-forth. The push. The loop. The "again, but tweak is this way..." The hundredth iteration where the thing finally clicks.
If you're a spectator to your own output, you are not the author of your own output. Get your hands in.
### 9. play with purpose. and play for play.
Both. At the same time.
Some days the play is in service of a thing.
Some days the play is the thing.
A practice that only ever has goals is a job. A practice that never has goals is a hobby. The good work lives in between. Play doesn't result in burnout. It results in excitement, happiness, experiment, the unexpected, and an urge to play more.
### 10. be a builder and an ideas person
The split is fake. It was always fake. It's especially fake now. The people who can think of the thing and make the thing are going to eat. The people who can only do one half are going to be very busy explaining why the other half is hard, or blame the processes or tools.
Don't be that person. Learn the other half. It's never been cheaper to learn it.
## things I am trying to stop doing
- waiting until it's "ready"
- editing in my head instead of on the page
- making but not sharing publicly
- taking briefs that secretly bore me
- pretending taste is an innate quality
- treating "AI" like a noun instead of a verb
## things I am trying to do more
- finish the bad version first
- show people the in-between, mess, experiments
- write the thing I'd want to read
- dig deeper, get help
- stop pretending I know stuff, ask dumber questions
- say the more specific thing
This file will be wrong in six months. That is fine.
I'd rather be specifically wrong than vaguely correct.
— b.
last touched, kitchen table, late.

articles.body:

6× Faster test suite
29m 56s → 5m 06s wall p95
“At Mastra we move so fast that the bottleneck becomes reviews and CI. Time spent compounds, and StarSling helps you realize how much time you're losing.”
Mastra case study
Up to 10x faster GitHub Actions runners with AI agents 
that continuously optimize your workflows
No credit card required
Agents write code faster than CI can check it. These teams made verification keep up.
3M+ CI jobs run
2× Faster E2E
2m 22s → 1m 04s
“We've been using StarSling for Better Auth CI. It's been saving us countless hours, both with fast runners and their agent optimizing our CI.”
16× Shorter queue time
9.5 min → 35 s
“Within a day of migrating to StarSling Runners, their agents opened up a PR that literally made our Rust CI tests 2x faster!”
Drop-in replacement for ubuntu-latest.
Install in a minute
Update your workflow file.
jobs:
  build:
    Removed: runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    Added: runs-on: starsling-ubuntu-26.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
Your workflow. A faster runner.
Every job, action and build command stays as written. Switch runners to see the line that changes and the median job time on each.
Get Started For Free
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
LatestIntroducing Adaptive Compute: up to 2.3x faster GitHub Actions
Sandbox Router sends every job to the fastest available sandbox, and Afterburner adds up to 25% more CPU and up to 50% more RAM to a running step at no extra cost. Up to 2.32x faster than GitHub-hosted runners.
Open source, one install, and they run on your machine: each skill reads your workflows and hands your coding agent the evidence to fix them.
33% cheaper than GitHub Actions
Volume discounts available
Everything you need to evaluate StarSling for your CI.
StarSling is AI-native CI for GitHub Actions: drop-in Ubuntu runners plus agents that open optimization PRs for your workflows. The runners replace ubuntu-latest and ubuntu-24.04 and run up to 33% cheaper than equivalent GitHub-hosted runners. Together with agent PRs, they made GitHub Actions up to 10x faster in public benchmarks, and the agents continuously analyze your workflows to keep the pipeline improving.
Agent-native CI is CI that improves itself. Beyond running your workflows on faster hardware, AI agents continuously analyze your jobs, run logs, and machine telemetry, then open pull requests that optimize your pipeline: caching, parallelization, dependency installs, test sharding, and workflow structure. Traditional CI is static; agent-native CI gets faster the longer you use it. Read more about AI-native CI.
Two things move the needle: faster hardware and removing redundant work. Swap ubuntu-latest for a runner with stronger CPUs, then let AI agents find dead steps, cache fixes, and parallelization opportunities your team hasn't had time to fix (in StarSling's public benchmarks, runners plus agent PRs made CI up to 10x faster). For a deeper guide, read fast GitHub Actions. You can also work through the GitHub Actions CI best practices yourself, without StarSling, or follow Levels of CI for every way to make GitHub Actions cheaper and faster.
Usually the runner. GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runs on older shared hardware, so even simple builds spend time waiting on CPU. Switching to faster CPUs (StarSling Runners use 5th Gen AMD EPYC) typically cuts wall-clock time significantly before any workflow optimization.
Yes. Change runs-on: ubuntu-latest to runs-on: starsling-ubuntu-26.04 (or ubuntu-24.04 to starsling-ubuntu-24.04) in your GitHub Actions workflow files. No other config changes required. See StarSling vs GitHub Actions and GitHub Actions alternatives.
StarSling is not a full replacement for GitHub Actions. It is a GitHub Actions runner alternative for supported Ubuntu/Linux jobs: you keep GitHub Actions workflows and change the runner label. If you are comparing full CI/CD platforms, read GitHub Actions alternatives.
$0.008 per minute for 4 vCPU Linux runners with 16 GB RAM, 33% cheaper than GitHub Actions' $0.012/min. New paid subscriptions are billed by the second, with no one-minute minimum. Queue time is never billed. New accounts get 2,000 free minutes in their first month. See StarSling pricing.
Yes. StarSling Disks are persistent directories mounted into StarSling Runners, so dependency stores and build output, such as pnpm's store or Rust's target/, are already in place when the next job starts. In a benchmark on Mastra's 4.5 GiB pnpm store, dependencies were ready in about 25 seconds, 4.5x faster than GitHub's actions/cache. Pull requests from the same repository read the default branch's published disk. Storage is $0.50 per GB-month.
StarSling Runners are x64 Linux, from 2 to 64 vCPU. Need ARM? Email founders@starsling.dev.
Building Docker images in CI? Email founders@starsling.dev to talk through caching layers on StarSling Runners.
Yes. StarSling GPU Runners are drop-in GitHub Actions runners backed by a dedicated NVIDIA GPU: RTX PRO 6000 at a normalized $0.06422 per minute, RTX 5090 at $0.03022, and RTX 4090 at $0.02522, with H100 coming soon. Set runs-on: starsling-ubuntu-26.04-gpu and pick a card in the label. The GPU is dedicated to that job for as long as it runs, so nothing reclaims it partway through your suite. Explore StarSling GPU Runners.
RTX PRO 6000 is the default, and it suits large-model and memory-heavy CI workloads. RTX 5090 suits fast inference tests and model evals. RTX 4090 covers everyday GPU tests at the lowest per-minute cost. You choose per job in the runs-on: label, so different jobs in the same workflow can use different cards. Explore StarSling GPU Runners.
Yes. StarSling Review Runners are code review agents you configure and run in your own CI. One workflow file, and every pull request is analyzed as a GitHub Actions job on a StarSling runner using your model key, review skills and scripts from your codebase, and team-defined reviewers. Skills and instructions load from the trusted base branch, so a pull request cannot rewrite its own reviewer. The output is a review comment on the pull request, before a human opens it. Explore StarSling Review Runners.
A review is a GitHub Actions job on a StarSling runner in the same account as the rest of your CI. It runs on starsling-review, a 4 vCPU runner with 16 GB of memory. Review Runner time has a normalized rate of $0.004 per minute. New paid subscriptions are billed in whole seconds from job start to finish. Partial seconds round up, with no one-minute minimum. Existing paid subscriptions remain billed in whole minutes with a one-minute minimum until migrated. Queue time is never billed. Concurrency is unlimited. Model tokens are billed by your own provider, on the account you already have. Explore StarSling Review Runners.
After installing the StarSling GitHub App, AI agents continuously analyze your workflows, jobs, run logs, and machine telemetry, then open pull requests that optimize your setup: cache fixes, faster install strategies, Docker health checks, test sharding, parallelization, workflow structure, and job ordering. You review and merge. Optimization PRs are on paid plans, off by default for new accounts.
Coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) push PR volume up several-fold, which compounds CI cost and queue times fast. The right fit is a runner with unlimited concurrency, continuous AI optimization (so the pipeline gets faster as PR volume grows), and per-minute pricing with no seat fees. StarSling Runners are built for this pattern.
Failed jobs are billed for the time they run: whole seconds on new paid subscriptions, with partial seconds rounded up; whole minutes on existing paid subscriptions until migrated. Queue time is never billed. New accounts get 2,000 free minutes in their first month.
Each job runs in its own single-use, hardware-isolated microVM that's destroyed after the run. That's the same isolation model GitHub-hosted runners use, so there's nothing for a later job or a fork PR to persist on or reach. Secrets pass directly from GitHub to your job and are never stored by StarSling. More details in our docs.
Sign up with GitHub and install the StarSling GitHub App, switch runners with one line, and run 2x faster on day one. StarSling agents keep finding the next speedup.

Set runs-on: starsling-ubuntu-26.04-gpu and pick a card in the label. The GPU is dedicated to that job for as long as it runs, so nothing reclaims it partway through your suite. Explore StarSling GPU Runners.
RTX PRO 6000 is the default, and it suits large-model and memory-heavy CI workloads. RTX 5090 suits fast inference tests and model evals. RTX 4090 covers everyday GPU tests at the lowest per-minute cost. You choose per job in the runs-on: label, so different jobs in the same workflow can use different cards. Explore StarSling GPU Runners.
Yes. StarSling Review Runners are code review agents you configure and run in your own CI. One workflow file, and every pull request is analyzed as a GitHub Actions job on a StarSling runner using your model key, review skills and scripts from your codebase, and team-defined reviewers. Skills and instructions load from the trusted base branch, so a pull request cannot rewrite its own reviewer. The output is a review comment on the pull request, before a human opens it. Explore StarSling Review Runners.
A review is a GitHub Actions job on a StarSling runner in the same account as the rest of your CI. It runs on starsling-review, a 4 vCPU runner with 16 GB of memory. Review Runner time has a normalized rate of $0.004 per minute. New paid subscriptions are billed in whole seconds from job start to finish. Partial seconds round up, with no one-minute minimum. Existing paid subscriptions remain billed in whole minutes with a one-minute minimum until migrated. Queue time is never billed. Concurrency is unlimited. Model tokens are billed by your own provider, on the account you already have. Explore StarSling Review Runners.
After installing the StarSling GitHub App, AI agents continuously analyze your workflows, jobs, run logs, and machine telemetry, then open pull requests that optimize your setup: cache fixes, faster install strategies, Docker health checks, test sharding, parallelization, workflow structure, and job ordering. You review and merge. Optimization PRs are on paid plans, off by default for new accounts.
Coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) push PR volume up several-fold, which compounds CI cost and queue times fast. The right fit is a runner with unlimited concurrency, continuous AI optimization (so the pipeline gets faster as PR volume grows), and per-minute pricing with no seat fees. StarSling Runners are built for this pattern.
Failed jobs are billed for the time they run: whole seconds on new paid subscriptions, with partial seconds rounded up; whole minutes on existing paid subscriptions until migrated. Queue time is never billed. New accounts get 2,000 free minutes in their first month.
Each job runs in its own single-use, hardware-isolated microVM that's destroyed after the run. That's the same isolation model GitHub-hosted runners use, so there's nothing for a later job or a fork PR to persist on or reach. Secrets pass directly from GitHub to your job and are never stored by StarSling. More details in our docs.
Sign up with GitHub and install the StarSling GitHub App, switch runners with one line, and run 2x faster on day one. StarSling agents keep finding the next speedup.

articles.title: Solid 2.0
articles.body:
Solid 2.0 - The Long Hold
Solid 2.0 reaches stable after five years: async in the reactive graph, server functions, diagnostics built for agents, and a smaller API.
5 years is a long time to work on anything. It took 5 years from my first commit of Solid to 1.0, and it's been another 5 since then.
A lot changes in 5 years. Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces. Back then it was an unusual position. Today signals are everywhere. In Angular, in Svelte's runes, in Vue Vapor, and in a proposal before TC39 to put them in the language itself. It even pushed the conversation into React's compiler.
More recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build. But Solid has always been about building the right things; the performant things. So for us the mission hasn't really changed all that much. The things that we identified as standout about our approach still stand out now. But instead of living in the shadow of more popular solutions Solid 2.0 carves out a path that others can follow. Deliberately this time.
Today that solution reaches stable.
Async Graph
If fine-grained reactivity's greatest strength is knowing the shape of our application, that knowledge shouldn't end with the process, or the machine the code is running on. Real applications are distributed. Real applications are born from data that lives on a server. The coordination of these pieces should be intentional and by design.
This starts with bringing async into the graph. A computation can return a Promise or an async iterator, and everything downstream just understands:
This allows authoring by affordance while automating the handling of race conditions. The introduction of async doesn't cause an app refactor. Speculative state is automatically rolled back without manually written processes ensuring the server remains the authority on truth.
SolidStart introduce the world to server functions in early 2022, and now they have found their way home to Solid's core, better than ever. Not only do they support highly capable RPC calls over Request/Response but persistent connections over Server Sent Events. And consuming it remains as simple as the code below.
This is only the beginning of what can be done with Server Functions and we will be announcing some new features (like reactive Server Components) in coming weeks that leverage this capability.
Built to Be Written by Agents
"But, we aren't writing the code anymore!" We hear you. A system built on constraints by construction ends up with less code to maintain and less edge cases. What used to be considered a DX shortcoming of reactive frameworks are now their greatest strength. And Solid 2.0 goes all in.
Every framework now says it "works great with AI", and usually that means models have seen a lot of it. That's a statement about training data, not about the framework. The question that matters is what happens when the agent gets it wrong.
In most frameworks a reactive mistake is silent. The app runs, it's just wrong, and the framework can't tell you, because it can't see it either. Solid can. A fine-grained graph knows exactly what was read, where, and what will update. So Solid 2.0's development builds report mistakes as they happen, with a stable code, the location in your source, and the fix:
These handle everything from strict errors to helpful heuristics. Thanks to async in the graph we can detect waterfalls, poorly constructed effect loops, poorly scaling graph shapes like wide graph fanouts and fan-ins. Today along with linting rules we can provide the best in class direction for agents at compile and at runtime.
This area is still evolving as we learn more about how agents build applications with Solid. The hard part, defining the primitives and semantics, is done. We've integrated with new dev tooling, and Chrome's Performance Tracks. And this capability goes beyond development as this observability powers things like our updated Sentry plugin so you can get the same information on your production builds.
We've also been looking at alternative syntax. Solid 2.0 adds experimental support for ReactiveScript and TSRX, both aiming to use compilation to further improve agent authoring.
One Framework for All
I've always been a big believer that React's super power is its composability. That it allowed the ecosystem to build on its humble pieces. However, we've learned a lot since 2013. At that point composable state, async patterns, and server rendering lacked the primitives to build upon and the ecosystem came up with their own solutions. This was fine for a while but tied React's hands and fractured their ecosystem. Something only a framework as popular as React could survive.
Newer frameworks have taken more on themselves and tend to only have one metaframework, or one router. We respect React's original positioning but have updated it for 2026. It isn't about restricting the solution but giving developers the primitives to build upon in the way React originally did. Server functions are example of this. Supporting any router, and cache solution for Single-Flight Mutation is another.
We retired our metaframework SolidStart, since every primitive needed to build a Solid Metaframework is now provided by the core or by framework agnostic Vite plugins. We believe that building an opinionated layer like a metaframework shouldn't have you needing to re-implement everything again. We've taken care of the hard parts so you can focus on what you care about. And these days a lot of that work is going to be taken on by your agent. This means less to maintain but no loss in capability.
And this makes it easier for the ecosystem. Solid 2.0 only requires one Clerk or Sentry plugin since we provide the primitives for Request/Response (built on web standards) and the hooks for observability that work across any library. We've already seen success with TanStack Query and Router being as capable as anything we've built first party, bringing in Tanner's impeccable attention to detail for the APIs people love to use.
Less is More
Somehow even though Solid 2.0 brings more capability to Solid, we've collapsed the surface area at almost every point. There are less primitives needed to be learnt, less ceremony around handling async. createResource, batch, startTransition, on, produce, createComputed, createMutable are all gone, because we no longer need them.
The equivalent code written for Solid 2.0 is shorter and clearer on intent. It informs our ability observe the runtime, provide better compiler errors, and removes the need for as many escape hatches (like createEffect) that can get us in trouble. This is something we believe important in an age of AI. Safe by construction rather than by exhaustion. Reduce complexity by deriving(reducing) state rather than putting it in a reducer.
When the framework carries the guarantees, all loading state, race conditions, and cancellation logic disappears and what you are left with is the UI.
The Road Here
The first discussions of what a Solid 2.0 would look like started at the moment 1.0 was released. We saught feedback from the community on new reactivity ideas. The real effort started in late 2024. We announced the road to 2.0 in February 2025. Over a year of experiments followed, rewriting the reactive core from scratch until the async model held up to everything we threw at it. The beta landed in March, and the Release Candidate in August, with the API frozen.
Then 23 release candidates in 14 weeks. In that time alone, 971 pull requests were merged and 753 issues closed. We set one bar for stable. A full week with no regression in ordinary app code, and no crash or hang anywhere. It took a while to get there. By the end, the bug reports coming in were from people(agents) deliberately hunting edge cases in the deepest corners of the scheduler, and finding them.
So many people have touched the project over the past 5 years, from working on the initial reactivity prototypes, to testing the latest RC builds on their production apps. I've tried to thank as many of you as I can and attached hundreds of handles in the RC announcement. There are so many. There are also the many great organizations that have sponsored our development over the years: Sentry, Netlify, Google Chrome, JetBrains, Anomaly, Cursor, Code Rabbit, Anthropic, Tembo and so many more.
But mostly I want to thank everyone who has believed in the project. We've accomplished great things and there is much more to come. That isn't possible without all of you. Personally, the past 2 and half years have been some of the most difficult of my life, but knowing what we are building that impacts so many people leaves me with a sense of fulfillment. Solid has always been bigger than its core team, and 2.0 is the clearest proof of that yet.
Solid 2.0 is here. Let's build.
The Long Hold refers to a diagnostic warning in Solid 2.0. It fires when a hold has been shown(isPending) but sufficient time has passed since the last input. Holds were at the heart of our async work for 2.0, and we acknowledge it took a while for this all to land.

articles.title: Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing
articles.body:
Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing
A savory cornbread base stuffing with Mexican chorizo, softened lightly browned onions, tender vegetables, and warm spices, baked until golden and lightly crisp on top.
Serves6 to 8
Prep20 minutes
Cook50 minutes to 55 minutes
Why You’ll Love Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing
- A fun twist on a holiday classic. This stuffing brings bold Mexican-inspired flavors to the holiday table while keeping everything you love about traditional stuffing.
- The texture is irresistible. The stuffing bakes up soft and tender in the center with lightly golden crisp edges.
- It’s easy to make ahead. The cornbread can be toasted in advance, making assembly a breeze when you’re preparing a big holiday meal.
Chorizo was always a staple in our Mexican American household. Whether it was tucked into a warm tortilla for breakfast or cooked alongside potatoes, it was one of those ingredients that always brought so much flavor to the table. So when it came to putting my own spin on a classic Thanksgiving stuffing, adding Mexican chorizo just made sense.
This chorizo cornbread stuffing brings together slightly sweet, tender cornbread with smoky chorizo, softened vegetables, and warm spices. The chorizo adds the best smoky, salty, and spicy bite, while the cornbread soaks up all those delicious flavors and bakes until golden and lightly crisp on top (my favorite part!). It’s a fun twist on a classic that deserves a spot on your holiday table, but it also makes a wonderful weeknight side dish whenever you’re craving something smoky and slightly sweet. Truly, it’s the best of all the worlds combined into one baking dish.
Straight from Our Recipe Tester
“This recipe has me convinced that chorizo was destined for cornbread stuffing. The heavily spiced, super-savory sausage is the perfect complement to sweet cornbread. I used a tray of cornbread from the grocery store bakery and it was such an easy shortcut I’ll definitely be repeating.” —Rachel, October 2026
Why You Should Trust Me
As a Mexican American recipe developer with over a decade of experience in professional kitchens and food media, I love finding ways to bring the flavors I grew up with into classic American dishes. This chorizo cornbread stuffing combines my love for traditional holiday comfort food with the bold, savory flavors of Mexican chorizo.
Key Ingredients in Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing
- Cornbread: Creates a slightly sweet, tender base that absorbs the savory flavors while developing lightly crisp edges as it bakes.
- Mexican chorizo: Adds a rich, smoky, slightly spicy flavor while the rendered fat seasons the vegetables and cornbread.
- Jalapeño: Adds a gentle kick of heat that balances the sweetness of the cornbread.
- Eggs: Bind the stuffing together, helping it hold its shape.
How to Make Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing
- Toast the cornbread. Bake the diced cornbread until lightly browned and dried.
- Cook the chorizo. Brown the chorizo in a large skillet, breaking into small pieces.
- Cook the vegetables. Add the onion, carrot, celery, jalapeño, and salt. Cook until softened, then stir in the garlic and spices.
- Combine the stuffing. Stir the toasted cornbread, followed by the whisked broth, eggs, and melted butter.
- Bake the stuffing. Transfer to a greased baking dish, top with cheese if using, and bake until golden-brown and set. Garnish with cilantro and freshly ground black pepper.
Helpful Swaps
- Store-bought or homemade cornbread both work well in this recipe. Just make sure it’s thoroughly dried out before assembling the stuffing.
- Swap pepper Jack for Monterey Jack if you want a milder, creamier finish, if using cheese.
Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing Recipe
A savory cornbread base stuffing with Mexican chorizo, softened lightly browned onions, tender vegetables, and warm spices, baked until golden and lightly crisp on top.
Prep time 20 minutes
Cook time 50 minutes to 55 minutes
Serves 6 to 8
Nutritional Info
Ingredients
- Cooking spray
- 6 cups diced store-bought or homemade cornbread (18 ounces)
- 1 pound Mexican chorizo, casings removed
- 1 medium yellow onion, small dice (1 1/4 cups)
- 1 medium carrot, peeled and small dice (1/2 cups)
- 1 medium stalk celery, small dice (1/2 cup)
- 1 medium jalapeño pepper, stemmed, seeded, and small dice (1/4 cup)
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt
- 1/2 teaspoon smoked paprika
- 1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, plus more for garnish
- 1 1/2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth
- 2 large eggs
- 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted
- 4 ounces pepper Jack or Monterey Jack cheese, shredded (1 cup, optional)
- Coarsely chopped fresh cilantro, for garnish (optional)
Instructions
- Heat the oven to 350ºF. Coat a 9x13-inch baking dish with cooking spray.
- Arrange 6 cups diced cornbread in an even layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Bake, stirring halfway through, until lightly brown, toasted, and dried out, 15 to 20 minutes total. Let cool slightly.
- Heat a large 12-inch skillet over medium heat. Add 1 pound Mexican chorizo and cook, breaking it up into small pieces and stirring occasionally, until browned and cooked through, 6 to 8 minutes.
- Stir in 1 small-diced medium yellow onion, 1 peeled and small-diced medium carrot, 1 small-diced medium celery stalk, 1 small-diced jalapeño pepper, and 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt. Cook until the vegetables are softened and the onion begins to brown, 8 to 10 minutes. Stir in 2 minced garlic cloves and cook until fragrant, about 40 seconds. Turn off the heat.
- Stir in 1/2 teaspoon smoked paprika and 1/4 teaspoon black pepper. Stir in the cornbread; it's OK if it begins to break or crumble up.
- Whisk 1 1/2 cups low-sodium chicken broth, 2 large eggs, and 2 tablespoons melted unsalted butter together in a medium bowl. Pour evenly over the cornbread mixture. Stir gently until combined and the broth mixture is absorbed.
- Transfer to the baking dish and arrange into an even layer. Sprinkle with 4 ounces shredded pepper Jack cheese if using.
- Bake until heated through and lightly browned on top, 20 to 25 minutes. Garnish with more black pepper and chopped fresh cilantro if desired.
Recipe Notes
Make ahead: The cornbread can be toasted up to 1 day ahead, cooled, and stored in an airtight container at room temperature.
Storage: Refrigerate leftover stuffing in an airtight container for up to 4 days.

articles.title: Phrack 73 Released
articles.body:
Title : Introduction
|=-----------------------------------------------------------------------=|
|=---------------------=[     Introduction     ]=------------------------=|
|=-----------------------------------------------------------------------=|
|=---------------------=[     Phrack Staff     ]=------------------------=|
|=---------------------=[   [email protected]   ]=------------------------=|
|=-----------------------------------------------------------------------=|
|=---------------------=[  September 30, 2026  ]=------------------------=|
|=-----------------------------------------------------------------------=|
--[ Past ]
Last year marked the 40th anniversary of Phrack so we went big. We published
our anniversary launch release in print at Defcon 33, HOPE, WHY25 and some
additional variations at several conferences around the world including
AlligatorCon, B-Sides Canberra, Out of the Box, Datenspuren, DistrictCon,
OffensiveCon, Recon, and Toorcamp. We included a CTF with exploit challenges
and had puzzles and easter eggs included in the zine. We threw parties and
had talks at Defcon and WHY25 to celebrate this milestone.
More importantly, we got new research into people's hands. The point of the
relaunch was to get people reading, researching, writing, and contributing
again. We wanted the next person picking up Phrack to find something that
made them sit down at a computer and start pulling a system apart.
We owe a huge thanks to the authors, editors, artists, publishing partners,
donors, and staff who made it happen. Writing the paper, working through
revisions, putting the print editions together, paying the bills, and
getting boxes of zines to the right places all take time and effort. Most of
that work is invisible when you are holding the finished issue. We
appreciate everyone who did it.
And to the readers: thank you for giving a shit. Seeing someone get excited
about an article, connect it to something they are working on, or realize
that they could contribute something themselves makes the effort worthwhile.
That exchange is how this thing keeps going. The relaunch worked, and this
issue is the follow-through.
--[ Present ]
This is the third release curated by the new staff, and we are not slowing
down. This issue is larger than last year's, with 23 main papers and eight
additional articles in Line Noise. The subjects range from exploitation and
reverse engineering to machine learning, hardware, and the history and
culture that grew around this work.
We have container escapes through the vDSO, use-after-free exploitation, QNX
userland shellcode, Linux kernel research, and a Chromium renderer sandbox
escape through Skia. Elsewhere, the issue takes on Windows smart card
architecture, static taint analysis in Binary Ninja, and autonomous
underwater vehicles.  There is also work examining backdoors in machine
learning and what it means to trust an AI system. One paper takes us from
PhrackCTF to two WinFSP zero-days, which is a pretty good argument for
continuing to put challenges in a zine.
We also have four more articles in Phrack World History, including the story
of the infamous SSH1 CRC32 vulnerability featured in The Matrix Reloaded as
well as stories about blue boxing free phone calls, a confession of a hacker
who tried to backdoor Linux kernel in 2003, and an early discovery of
botnets for hire. Our Prophile features Halvar Flake, whose contributions to
reverse engineering and security research are legendary.
--[ Future ]
In 2026, we find ourselves in a time of rapid technological change. It is
hard to say what vulnerability research or red teaming will look like in
another five years. AI has moved well beyond completing a line of code into
agentic systems capable of analyzing source code and reverse engineering
binaries to find and exploit vulnerabilities.
We can be sure that the future will require us to continue to explore new
ideas, create new tools, and push the boundaries of what is possible in the
face of new challenges and opportunities created by the advancement of AI
and automation systems. As the effort required to put ideas into practice
falls, creativity and human intuition forged through experience is valued
even higher.
We hope that this release of Phrack will inspire new ideas, discussions, and
collaborations that will keep the human side of hacking a critical element
in shaping the future of technology and society. We will continue to do our
part to support the community and provide a platform for sharing knowledge
and ideas. We look forward to seeing what the future holds and we are
excited to be a part of it.
Read the papers, try the ideas, and challenge the conclusions. When you find
something worth sharing, write it up and send it in. We have another issue
to put together, and some of you should be in it!
--[ Greetz ]
To those who have supported us the past three years helping to restore
vitality to Phrack, we thank you.
Conferences who funded prints: Defcon, OffensiveCon, Recon, Unprompted[AU],
Unprompted[US], BSides Canberra, Alligatorcon, TenguCon
Sponsors & Major Donors - WatchTowr, Elltam, Verichains, BShield,
TrustedSec, Binarly, Trenchant, Praetorian (WWSUL), EFF, Blaze, EMX,
Mullvad, ToorCon, Hacker Initiative, Endrazine, Dug Song, Napster, halvar,
Horizon, Huku, Julio Auto, Gadi, and the rest of the people who stepped up with
smaller donations.
Artists - Ian Dash, pinguino, tainted, pepper, mar, xer0, abstrakt, ToscaKaiser,
h7, zir, Mick, p0rtL, netspooky, ackmage, digitalis, Tedsig42, and the many
others who submitted their work for consideration.
Reviewers - barbie, bsdaemon, C, chompie, danielcuthbert, devinc, grugq, joern,
jordan9001, K3, richinseattle, roddux, saber, skyper, SSHad0w, TMZ, zh4ck
All the authors past and present who are now bound to the history of phrack.
The unnamed ones who have helped us with logistics and carrying literal tons
of paper around conferences to deliver them into the hands of the next
generation.
